Article Title: A Tennessee couple said nearly 30 years of mowing, gardening and holding yard sales gave them ownership of a strip next to their home; on October 29, an appeals court ruled that the developer owned th
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How the property dispute began

Why the couple claimed ownership

Why the appeals court rejected their claim

Court upholds the developer's rights

Using a piece of land for decades can create a strong sense of ownership, especially when people regularly maintain it, plant gardens and use it for everyday activities. However, long-term use does not automatically establish legal ownership. A Tennessee couple who claimed that a strip of land beside their home belonged to them after nearly 30 years of maintenance have lost their legal battle, with an appeals court ruling in favour of the developer.In its October 29, 2026, decision in Developed by Design, LLC v. James M. Travis et al., available on Justia, the Tennessee Court of Appeals upheld a lower court's ruling that the disputed land belonged to the development company. The court found that James M Travis and his wife, Mary M Travis, had failed to establish ownership through adverse possession. Their activities, including mowing, gardening and holding yard sales, were not sufficient to satisfy the legal requirements.The dispute involved Developed by Design, LLC, which had acquired approximately 43.39 acres of undeveloped land in Rhea County, Tennessee. The company planned to develop the property, which was located next to the Travises' home.The disagreement began in 2021 when James Travis objected to work being carried out near his property. He believed the company was crossing the boundary and interfering with land that his family had used for years. The developer maintained that the boundary shown in its property records was correct. It relied on a survey prepared by Jack B. Kimsey in 1966 and recorded in the Rhea County Register of Deeds in April 1967.On June 14, 2023, the company filed a lawsuit seeking to establish the correct boundary and confirm its rights to a 30-foot right-of-way across the Travises' property. It also requested an injunction preventing the couple from interfering with its use of the access route. The couple challenged the company's position and filed a counterclaim, arguing that they had acquired ownership of the disputed strip through adverse possession.James Travis testified that his family had treated the disputed area as part of their property since purchasing their home in 1996. He described activities including mowing the grass, using weed trimmers, clearing walking paths, spreading gravel and maintaining a garden. They had also planted blueberry bushes, held yard sales and stored various belongings in the area.The couple argued that these activities demonstrated continuous and exclusive use of the land for more than the 20-year period required under Tennessee's common-law adverse possession principles. However, the development company disputed their claims. Its representative, Caleb Yawn, testified that he had observed a garden near the boundary but believed it was located on the Travises' side of the surveyed property line. Yawn also said that several objects, including a car door, kitchen sink, bicycle and old pipes, appeared in the disputed area after the disagreement began in 2021. He testified that, to his knowledge, the Travises had not begun mowing the disputed area until 2021. The trial court also questioned the credibility of James Travis's testimony concerning the couple's use of the disputed land.Under Tennessee law, adverse possession requires proof of actual, exclusive, adverse, continuous, open and notorious possession for the required period. The claim must be established through clear and convincing evidence. The appeals court found that the Travises had not satisfied these requirements. Although the couple had maintained and used the area, the judges concluded that mowing grass, gardening and planting bushes did not demonstrate the necessary degree of control over the property.The court also examined whether their use was sufficiently open and notorious. This means that the actual owner must have known about the possession or that the activities must have been visible enough to provide notice of the ownership claim. The couple had not installed fences or no-trespassing signs to indicate that they considered the disputed area exclusively theirs. Their daughter, Olivia Keller, also testified that there was nothing on the land indicating that it belonged to her parents.The court further found that the couple had not demonstrated exclusive possession against competing ownership claims. Regularly maintaining an area was not enough to establish that they had exercised legal control over it.Judge Thomas R. Frierson II delivered the appeals court's opinion, joined by Chief Judge Frank G Clement Jr. and Judge Steven W Maroney. The court affirmed the lower court's October 20, 2025, judgment in all respects. This confirmed the boundary line presented by Developed by Design and its right to use the 30-foot right-of-way. The case was remanded to the trial court for execution of the judgment and collection of costs. The appeals court also assessed the costs of the appeal against James and Mary Travis.The ruling highlights an important distinction in property law: using and maintaining land for decades does not automatically make someone its legal owner. A person claiming ownership through adverse possession must establish that their actions meet every legal requirement, rather than relying solely on the length of time they have used the property.
Article Summary: The dispute involved Developed by Design, LLC, which had acquired approximately 43.39 acres of undeveloped land in Rhea County, Tennessee. The company planned to develop the property, which was located next to the Travises' home. The disagreement began in 2021 when James Travis objected to work being carried out near his property. He believed the company was crossing the boundary and interfering with land that his family had used for years. The couple argued that they had acquired ownership of the disputed strip through adverse possession.

Article Title: Arnold Schwarzenegger’s October charity night raised a record $9.75 million for After-School All-Stars, which provides free programmes for nearly 150,000 students across the United States
Article Text:
Arnold Schwarzenegger’s charity night raises record $9.75 million for US students (Image Credit: The Schwarzenegger Climate Initiative)

Arnold Schwarzenegger’s annual charity event raises $9.75 million

What happened during the 13th annual charity night?

How After-School All-Stars supports students

Schwarzenegger's long-standing commitment to the organisation

A single evening of fundraising can make a difference in the lives of thousands of children, particularly when it helps provide access to education, mentorship and opportunities beyond the classroom. Actor and former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger’s annual charity event in Los Angeles has achieved a new milestone, raising a record $9.75 million to support young people across the United States. The money will benefit After-School All-Stars, a non-profit organisation that works with children and young people through free after-school programmes.The Schwarzenegger Climate Initiative reported the record-breaking fundraising achievement in an October 14, 2026, update, noting that the annual Arnold Schwarzenegger–Westime Charity Night brought together supporters for a cause close to the actor’s heart. After-School All-Stars also confirmed the achievement in an October 22 post on its official website, describing the event as its 13th annual charity night. The organisation said the funds would support its nationwide programmes, which serve nearly 150,000 students.The 13th Annual Arnold Schwarzenegger-Westime Charity Night was held earlier in October at Schwarzenegger’s home in Los Angeles. The event was co-hosted by Schwarzenegger and John Simonian, founder of luxury watch retailer Westime and a board member of After-School All-Stars.The fundraiser has developed into an important annual gathering for supporters of the organisation. What began as an effort to bring friends and supporters together has grown into a major fundraising occasion, with contributions directed towards programmes for children and young people.This year's total of $9.75 million marks a record for the event. According to After-School All-Stars, the amount represents an investment in the futures of nearly 150,000 students who benefit from its programmes across the country. The organisation emphasised that the fundraising achievement was not simply about collecting a large sum of money. It was about sustaining opportunities for students to discover their interests, develop confidence and work towards their personal and educational goals.The evening brought together supporters, entertainers, artists and contributors for a Western-themed celebration. The programme featured several performances and activities, giving guests an opportunity to participate in the fundraising effort while supporting the organisation's work. According to After-School All-Stars' account of the event, the entertainment included line dancing and performances by the two-time Grammy Award-winning Mariachi Divas. Young mariachi performer Mateo Lopez also presented a rendition of the US national anthem, while blues music brought the evening to a close.Guests were offered additional experiences, including customised Western hats, bolo ties and traditional tintype portraits. The event also featured a live auction, with individuals, artists and business partners contributing special items and experiences to help raise funds. Milan Carter served as the evening's emcee, while Chuck Dukas led the auction. Contributors included Richard Mille, MANSORY, boxer Ryan Garcia, Billy Lucas and Daniel Marshall. Artists Nick Moss, Lotte Zhang, Wes Lang and Hiro Yamagata also donated original works of art. The dining arrangements were provided by Wolfgang Puck Catering, with chefs Eric Klein and Garry Larduinat and their team overseeing the food. TOMA also returned to serve its signature empanadas.Co-founded by Schwarzenegger more than three decades ago, After-School All-Stars focuses on helping children succeed academically and develop skills that can support them beyond school. Its programmes provide free after-school and summer learning opportunities to students across the United States. The organisation operates at more than 750 schools and community sites nationwide. Its work includes academic support, enrichment activities, opportunities to build friendships and access to caring adults who can guide and encourage young people.These programmes are particularly important because learning and personal development do not stop when the regular school day ends. After-school activities can give children additional time to explore subjects, discover interests and develop abilities that may not receive as much attention during classroom lessons. By keeping programmes free, After-School All-Stars also aims to make these opportunities accessible to children and families who might otherwise face financial barriers to participation.In its October 22 announcement, the organisation highlighted the importance of relationships between students and programme staff. CEO Ben Paul explained that children often remember the people who made a difference in their lives more than individual activities. He emphasised that supportive relationships are central to the organisation's mission of helping young people succeed in school and life.Schwarzenegger's involvement in After-School All-Stars is closely connected to the organisation's founding and its continued efforts to expand opportunities for young people. Through the annual charity night, he has helped bring together donors and supporters to provide financial backing for its work. The latest fundraiser also reflects the role that private contributions and community support can play in sustaining non-profit programmes. While the $9.75 million raised represents a significant achievement, the organisation's work continues throughout the year at schools and community locations across the country.The Schwarzenegger Climate Initiative also highlighted the enthusiasm and generosity of those attending the event. Its director, Monika Langthaler, was present at the gathering and witnessed the support shown for the cause. With its latest fundraising record, the Arnold Schwarzenegger-Westime Charity Night has provided fresh support for an organisation working to make after-school education and enrichment opportunities available to nearly 150,000 students nationwide.
Article Summary: The 13th Annual Arnold Schwarzenegger-Westime Charity Night was held earlier in October at Schwarzenegger’s home in Los Angeles. The event was co-hosted by Schwarzenegger and John Simonian, founder of luxury watch retailer Westime and a board member of After-School All-Stars. The evening brought together supporters, entertainers, artists and contributors for a Western-themed celebration. The money will support its nationwide programmes, which serve nearly 150,000 students.

Article Title: Best-selling author James Patterson has given more than $220 million to literacy and education, endowing over 1,000 scholarships; his giving now reaches students, teachers, libraries and independent b
Article Text:
James Patterson (Image Credit: ALA)

A philanthropy built around reading

scholarship (Representative image)

Scholarships that change direction

Support for teachers and literacy research

Libraries and independent booksellers

Why Patterson’s giving stands out

A legacy beyond the bestsellers

James Patterson is best known as one of the world’s most successful thriller writers, but his most consequential work may be happening far from the bestseller lists. Through a long-running commitment to literacy and education, Patterson has given more than $220 million to support readers, teachers, writers, libraries and independent booksellers, according to his official Giving Back page. His philanthropy has also endowed more than 1,000 scholarships at colleges and universities across the United States. The scale of that giving is unusual, but so is its breadth. Patterson’s support does not focus only on students or only on schools. It reaches the entire ecosystem that makes reading possible, from classroom teachers and librarians to authors, literacy researchers and the independent bookshops that connect communities with books. His stated belief is simple: reading changes lives, and better readers make better humans. Read more about his initiative here:Patterson’s approach begins with the idea that literacy is not a single issue but a chain of connected needs. A child needs effective reading instruction, a teacher needs training and resources, a school library needs books, a writer needs support and a local bookshop needs customers and stability. His giving reflects that understanding by funding people and institutions at every stage of the reading journey.The author has contributed more than $220 million to literacy-focused philanthropy to date, as per details on his official website.That figure includes grants and programmes for educators, writers, authors and librarians, as well as major support for literacy organisations and research-based reading instruction. The aim is not merely to distribute books, but to strengthen the conditions that help children become confident, capable readers.This focus is especially significant because reading ability shapes nearly every later opportunity in education and work. A student who struggles to read early can face widening difficulties in comprehension, confidence and academic progress. Patterson’s philanthropy therefore treats literacy as a long-term investment in opportunity rather than a short-term charitable gesture.One of the most visible parts of Patterson’s giving is his scholarship programme. He has endowed more than 1,000 scholarships at universities nationwide, giving students financial support to pursue higher education and careers in teaching, writing and public service.The scholarships include substantial support for historically Black colleges and universities. According to Patterson’s website, more than 600 scholarships have been endowed at HBCUs, making this one of the most important strands of his educational philanthropy. These awards can reduce financial pressure at a critical point in a student’s life and help more young people complete degrees that might otherwise be out of reach.The emphasis on teaching, writing and public service is also deliberate. By supporting students who may enter classrooms, newsrooms, public institutions or creative fields, Patterson is investing in the people who shape communities after they graduate. A scholarship is not only help with tuition; it can be the first step toward a career that creates further opportunity for others.Patterson has directed more than $50 million to educators, writers, authors and librarians through grants and programmes. This support recognises that teachers and librarians often work with limited budgets while carrying enormous responsibility for children’s learning and access to books.His giving also includes major donations to the University of Florida Literacy Institute, known as UFLI. The institute focuses on evidence-based reading instruction, an approach that uses research on how children learn to read in order to improve classroom outcomes. Patterson’s support for UFLI places his philanthropy alongside efforts to improve reading instruction at scale, rather than relying only on individual donations or one-time book giveaways, as per the website.That matters because reading instruction has become one of the most urgent issues in American education. Many children arrive at school without the foundational skills needed to read fluently, and teachers need practical, research-backed methods to help them catch up. By funding literacy research and instruction, Patterson’s giving aims to improve outcomes for children who may never know his name.Librarians occupy a central place in Patterson’s vision of literacy. They provide free access to books, internet access, study space and programmes for children and adults, often in communities where such resources are scarce. Patterson’s support for libraries acknowledges that a strong public reading culture depends on institutions that welcome everyone, regardless of income.Independent booksellers also receive a place in his giving. Patterson has provided more than $3 million in support to independent bookstores, businesses that often operate on narrow margins but play an outsized role in local literary life. They recommend books, host authors, support school partnerships and give readers a physical place to discover stories.This support is notable because independent bookshops compete with online retailers and large chains. Patterson’s grants recognise that a healthy literary culture is not created by publishers and authors alone. It also depends on the shops, libraries and local champions who put the right book into the right reader’s hands.Many authors support literacy, but few have combined personal wealth, publishing influence and sustained giving at this scale. Patterson’s philanthropy is distinctive because it treats reading as a shared public project. It funds students, but also the educators, researchers, librarians and booksellers who make literacy possible every day.His approach also avoids treating books as a luxury. Patterson’s website frames reading as a pathway to opportunity, and his giving is designed to expand access for people who face financial or educational barriers. Whether through scholarships, teacher grants, library support or literacy research, the underlying goal is the same: help more people become readers and give them the tools to build better lives.There is also a practical lesson in the way the giving is structured. Rather than choosing one high-profile cause, Patterson has invested across the literacy system. That makes his philanthropy harder to summarise, but potentially more durable, because it strengthens the people and institutions that support readers long after a single grant or scholarship ends.James Patterson’s books have sold in enormous numbers, but his Giving Back page suggests that his longer-term legacy may rest on something quieter: children learning to read, students attending university, teachers receiving support and local bookshops staying open. More than $220 million has gone into that work, alongside more than 1,000 endowed scholarships and substantial support for HBCUs, literacy research, libraries and independent booksellers.The scale is remarkable, but the purpose is easy to understand. Patterson believes that reading changes lives, and his philanthropy is built to make that belief real for as many people as possible. In a world where access to books, good teaching and higher education remains uneven, his giving offers a model of how successful creators can use their resources to strengthen the foundations of opportunity.
Article Summary: The author has contributed more than $220 million to literacy-focused philanthropy to date. His philanthropy has also endowed more than 1,000 scholarships at colleges and universities across the United States. Patterson’s approach begins with the idea that literacy is not a single issue but a chain of connected needs.

Article Title: An Indiana doctor cut her hours to care for her newborn and reported earning $6,677 a week, but her divorce court calculated her earning capacity at $8,811 a week; an appeals court has upheld the ruli
Article Text:
Ashraf reduced her workload to three-quarters of a full-time schedule to look after their daughter (AI image)

Why court calculated income higher

Dispute over overnight stays with father

Appeals court upholds both decisions

An Indiana doctor who reduced her working hours to care for her newborn daughter has lost her appeal against a divorce court's decision to calculate her weekly earning capacity at $8,811, despite her reporting an income of $6,677 a week. The Indiana Court of Appeals ruled on Thursday siad that the lower court had sufficient evidence to conclude that Aiza Ashraf, a radiologist, was capable of working full-time. The judges also upheld an order allowing her former husband, Mohsin Mukhtar, to spend three nights a week with their young daughter.Ashraf and Mukhtar, both radiologists employed by Indiana University, married in 2018 and welcomed their daughter in August 2024, according to the case details available on Justia . Ashraf filed for divorce the following month. The couple's separation led to disagreements over their daughter's care, parenting time, and the income that should be considered when calculating child support.Both doctors received payments from Indiana University for teaching and from IU Health for providing medical services. They also had opportunities to earn additional money by taking extra shifts, commonly referred to as "moonlighting". Before taking maternity leave, Ashraf earned the same base salary as her husband.However, in January 2025, Ashraf reduced her workload to three-quarters of a full-time schedule to look after their daughter.She told the court that her gross weekly income was $6,677. Mukhtar argued that she could still earn the same base salary as him if she returned to full-time work.During the divorce proceedings, Ashraf explained that she specialised in breast imaging radiology and planned to maintain her credentials in that field rather than general diagnostic radiology.She said opportunities for additional shifts were limited because breast imaging was generally performed during regular working hours.Mukhtar disagreed. He told the court that both had the same employment contract and that Ashraf retained the training, qualifications and licence needed to perform general radiology work.He asked the court to calculate both parents' weekly income at $8,811, excluding earnings from additional shifts.On October 13, last year, the Hamilton Circuit Court accepted that Ashraf could work full-time and assessed her earning capacity at $8,811 per week.Ashraf challenged the decision, arguing that she had reduced her hours to care for her daughter rather than to avoid financial responsibilities.The appeals court examined whether the lower court had acted improperly by using her potential earnings instead of her reported income.Under Indiana's child support rules, courts can consider what a parent is capable of earning when that parent is voluntarily unemployed or working fewer hours than their qualifications and opportunities would allow.The appeals judges noted that Ashraf had acknowledged she could work additional hours if she wanted. They also considered evidence that she previously earned the same base salary as Mukhtar.The court rejected her argument that the $8,811 figure improperly included her husband's additional earnings. Both parents' financial documents identified that amount as his base weekly pay, excluding extra shifts.The case also involved a disagreement over how much time Mukhtar should spend with their daughter. According to the judgment, both parents initially helped care for the baby after her birth. However, in September 2024, Ashraf began sleeping in the nursery and prevented Mukhtar from entering the room.A preliminary court order issued in December 2024 did not allow overnight stays with the father. It provided that he could request them when the child turned six months old or began eating solid food.Mukhtar subsequently requested more time with his daughter, but Ashraf refused. On one occasion, she left the child with her maternal grandmother in Texas for two nights rather than arrange overnight care with Mukhtar.At the final divorce hearing in March 2025, Ashraf proposed gradually increasing the father's parenting time, with overnight stays beginning when their daughter turned two.She explained that she intended to continue breastfeeding until that age and wanted to be available to comfort the child at night.Mukhtar sought equal parenting time, including overnight stays. He told the court that he had participated in the baby's early care, regularly exercised his permitted parenting time and completed parenting courses.The lower court eventually awarded him three days of parenting time each week, including overnight stays.Ashraf challenged the overnight arrangement, arguing that the immediate increase from no overnight stays to three per week was not in their daughter's best interests.The appeals court acknowledged that the arrangement went beyond the usual recommendations under Indiana's parenting time guidelines for young children.However, it found that the lower court had considered the circumstances of the family, including Mukhtar's involvement in childcare, his completion of parenting courses and his ability to provide suitable accommodation.The judges also considered the lower court's concern that a gradual increase in parenting time might not happen because Ashraf had previously refused additional visits. The appeals court therefore concluded that the lower court had sufficient grounds to approve the arrangement.
Article Summary: Aiza Ashraf reduced her workload to three-quarters of a full-time schedule to look after their daughter. She told the court that her gross weekly income was $6,677. The couple's separation led to disagreements over their daughter's care, parenting time, and the income that should be considered when calculating child support.

Article Title: Meet Richard Andino, the nine-year-old California boy who turned two planter boxes into a successful vegetable business at his local farmers’ market in Loomis
Article Text:
Image: canva

How a family company and county approval took a boy’s vegetable stand to the Loomis Farmers Market

Why Richard would rather play outside than watch screens, and what his mother saw in kindergarten

What a paediatrician says about screen time, sleep, mood and behaviour in today’s children

Nine-year-old gardener and young entrepreneur Richard Andino, from Loomis in Placer County, California, has turned a simple school lesson about growing plants into a thriving vegetable business. He started with two planter boxes, a handful of vegetables, and plenty of curiosity, driven by a lifelong love of vegetables and a desire to sell them. Three years on, his garden is nearly three times its original size, because it has grown a little bigger every year. On harvest days, he carefully checks which crops are ripe before preparing to serve customers, a routine that fills his summer holidays.Richard’s first customers bought from a stand in front of his home. Today he is a regular vendor at the Loomis Farmers Market, a step that required his family to form a limited liability company and complete the county approval process for selling there, CBS News Sacramento reported.The money Richard earns covers summer activities such as Sky Zone and Sunsplash. Once he reaches his savings goal, he gives whatever remains of his harvest to members of the community.For Richard, time outdoors matters more than the income. He told CBS News Sacramento that he is not a big fan of screens and would rather play outside.His mother, Kabryna Andino, told the same outlet that the preference grew out of his early school years. In kindergarten, she said, he began suffering from very bad migraines, which she linked to being indoors and watching too many screens.Richard’s story comes as paediatricians continue to study how greater screen time affects children’s health. Amanda Mitchell, a paediatrician at Kaiser Roseville, told the outlet that heavy screen use changes the quality of children’s sleep, which in turn alters their mood and behaviour.She added that technology need not shape a whole generation. Children growing up in this era are overcoming its effects and becoming who they are meant to be, she said, and while technology helps them, it “does not define them”.Day to day, Richard tends the garden, talks with customers and grows something he built himself. He told the outlet that anyone who wants to run a business must expect challenges along the way. His advice is to keep going through each one, and success will follow.
Article Summary: Richard Andino, from Loomis in Placer County, California, has turned a simple school lesson about growing plants into a thriving vegetable business. He started with two planter boxes, a handful of vegetables, and plenty of curiosity, driven by a lifelong love of vegetables and a desire to sell them. Three years on, his garden is nearly three times its original size, because it has grown a little bigger every year.

Article Title: Maldives opposition's possible presidential pick Abdulla Shahid held in child abuse case
Article Text:
Shahid served as the Maldives' foreign affairs minister between 2018 and 2023 under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. During this period, he also became one of the country's most recognisable faces in international diplomacy.

Shahid rejects allegations

Who is Abdulla Shahid, Muizzu's potential challenger

Shahid's political position and MDP's preparations for 2028

Former Maldives foreign affairs minister Abdulla Shahid, was arrested on suspicion of sexually abusing a minor, the Maldives Police said on Monday. Notably, the 64-year-old former president of the United Nations General Assembly who was emerging as a potential presidential challenger to incumbent Mohamed Muizzu in the 2028 elections.He was taken into custody in Malé at around 9.59pm local time on Monday under a court warrant. Shahid has rejected the allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated.The arrest comes at a crucial time for the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), which is preparing for the next presidential election. Shahid was considered one of the prominent contenders for the party's presidential nomination.The Maldives Police confirmed the arrest in a statement posted on X."On suspicion of sexually abusing a child under the age of 18, Abdulla Shahid (64 yrs), H. Rabee’ee Manzil, Malé, was arrested under a court warrant on the night of 2 November 2026, at around 21:59. The police are currently conducting further investigations into this case," the police said.The police have not disclosed further details about the allegations.They said investigations into the case are continuing.Following his arrest, Shahid denied the allegations and accused those circulating the claims of attempting to damage his reputation.In a post on X, he said: "The stories being politically circulated to assassinate my character are completely baseless lies. I urge everyone to refrain from spreading such unsubstantiated claims,"The former minister has not publicly provided further details about the allegations or the circumstances leading to his arrest.The police have also not shared additional information about the case.Shahid is among the Maldives' most prominent political figures and has held several senior positions in the country's government and political establishment.He served as the Maldives' foreign affairs minister between 2018 and 2023 under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. During this period, he also became one of the country's most recognisable faces in international diplomacy.His most prominent international role came when he presided over the 76th session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) during 2021-22.He was also the Speaker of the People's Majlis, the Maldives' parliament, and headed the opposition MDP from February 2024 until August 2026.Shahid stepped down as MDP president in August 2026 to contest the party's presidential primary. He was subsequently seen as a prominent potential candidate for the party's nomination ahead of the 2028 presidential election.The arrest could therefore have significant political implications for the opposition party as it prepares to challenge President Mohamed Muizzu.The MDP is one of the Maldives' principal political parties and was in power under former president Ibrahim Mohamed Solih from 2018 to 2023.Solih lost the 2023 presidential election to Muizzu, who contested as the candidate of the People's National Congress (PNC).With the next presidential election scheduled for 2028, the opposition has been preparing to regain power. Shahid's international profile and experience in government had placed him among the prominent names being considered for the party's presidential nomination.However, the criminal allegations and his arrest could complicate his political prospects. The investigation is still underway, and the allegations against him have not been established.
Article Summary: Former Maldives foreign affairs minister Abdulla Shahid, was arrested on suspicion of sexually abusing a minor. Shahid has rejected the allegations, calling them baseless and politically motivated. The arrest comes at a crucial time for the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), which is preparing for the next presidential election.

Article Title: US launches 'secret' strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island amid Netanyahu push for post-midterm attacks
Article Text:
US launches 'secret' strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island as peace talks teeter along

The United States launched "secret" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing US officials, amid renewed tensions over the possibility of fresh military action against Tehran.The attack triggered a series of explosions on the island, located in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media outlet IRNA reported.The strikes were part of a series of limited military operations carried out by Washington in recent weeks, the WSJ said, adding that the attacks had been deliberately kept secret and conducted on a smaller scale to avoid signalling an intention to resume its broader military campaign against Iran.The developments came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly pressed US President Donald Trump to consider fresh military action against Iran after Tuesday's US midterm elections.Trump and Netanyahu held a telephone conversation on Saturday to discuss Washington's negotiations with Tehran and the possibility of resuming military operations, Axios reported, citing one Israeli and one US source.Follow live updates: ‘Hands stained with blood’ - Iran warns employees of 3 firms over alleged Israeli military links According to the report, Netanyahu urged Trump to launch fresh strikes after the elections, while the US president wanted to allow diplomatic efforts to continue for now. An Israeli source described the conversation as "tough", while a US source called it "direct".Earlier on Monday, Trump cast doubt on whether he would follow through on his threat to resume military strikes against Iran, while indicating that a diplomatic agreement remained possible.Asked by reporters whether he was considering striking Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections, Trump replied, "No."US Vice President JD Vance on Monday expressed optimism that Washington and Tehran could still reach a deal to prevent President Donald Trump from ordering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei last week, but the White House has shared few details about its contents. Trump said the letter focused on helping Iran with "medical supplies and various things"."We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians," Vance told reporters, adding that he had spoken to Trump about the matter."The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We're going to keep on working at it," he said.The US and Iran have been at war since February 28, with Washington and Tehran continuing to explore the possibility of a diplomatic settlement even as tensions remain high.
Article Summary: US launched'secret' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, WSJ reports. Attack triggered a series of explosions on the island, Iranian state media outlet IRNA reported. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly pressed US President Donald Trump to consider fresh military action against Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections.

Article Title: Florida jet 'broke apart' midair before crashing into roadway; 20-year-old pilot among victims
Article Text:
The aircraft eventually plunged at a rate of around 27,000 feet per minute

Ice, turbulence under scanner as jet plunges

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the aircraft's descent rate could be attributed to a loss of control? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Tech entrepreneur, family among nine victims

A Learjet 60 carrying nine people may have started breaking apart mid-air before plunging into a Florida roadway and erupting into a fireball, federal investigators said on Monday. The aircraft was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday when it suddenly went into a steep nosedive, leaving behind a crater and a widespread debris field near West Palm Beach.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said investigators were examining whether severe weather, ice accumulation and turbulence contributed to the crash, while also looking into possible mechanical problems and the actions of the flight crew. The victims included 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, as well as three other passengers. The pilot was identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory.NTSB member Tom Chapman said investigators had found indications that the aircraft began breaking apart before impact, raising the possibility that debris could be scattered across a considerable distance from the crash site.“We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site," Chapman said.Weather conditions are expected to be a major focus of the investigation. During the flight, the crew reported icing conditions at an altitude of around 35,000 feet, with temperatures reaching minus 47 degrees Celsius. The pilots also reported moderate turbulence and precipitation before requesting clearance to climb to 37,000 feet to avoid the weather.Air traffic controllers had warned the crew about approaching storms as the aircraft crossed into Florida. However, the plane subsequently began losing altitude at an alarming rate.According to recordings of air traffic control communications, the crew declared a mayday as the aircraft began descending at around 8,000 feet per minute. The rate increased to 20,000 feet per minute, with the pilot warning that the aircraft was in an overspeed condition.“We’re going to crash into the ground!” the pilot told air traffic control in one of the final transmissions.The aircraft eventually plunged at a rate of around 27,000 feet per minute, according to flight-tracking data, before communications were lost.AccuWeather said the tops of some storm clouds in the region reached 45,000 feet, potentially making it difficult for aircraft to fly over the storm system. Former NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration investigator Jeff Guzzetti said key components of the jet's tail may have been lost during the turbulence or steep descent, potentially making the aircraft impossible to control.“That very well could explain the missile-like profile just before it hit the ground," he said.Investigators are also hoping to recover the aircraft's cockpit voice recorder to establish what happened in its final moments. However, heavy rainfall has complicated the operation, with the impact crater partially filled with water.“This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said.The victims included Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp and their children Emma and Charlie. The family was travelling with Rachel Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina, according to a joint statement released by relatives.Robinson was a technology entrepreneur who founded and led companies including RB2B and Retention.com. He had previously worked at financial services firm Lehman Brothers and banking group Barclays.The family statement described Robinson and Sharp as "devoted parents", adding that their children were "the light of their lives"."Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," it said.Sharp was an artist and ceramics entrepreneur. Her father, Dudley Sharp, told The Palm Beach Post that the news had come as a devastating shock."We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane," he said.Reed and Fehr were described in the family statement as "full of joy and adventure". Cetina, meanwhile, was said to have cared for the couple's children with "tenderness and devotion", adding that she was "truly part of the family".The other two victims were the flight crew. Gregory, 55, was identified as the pilot by East Coast Jets, a private charter company where he had briefly worked in 2016 and 2017.Filgueiras, the 20-year-old co-pilot, was identified by her mother, Camila Corteleti, who confirmed her daughter's death to US media. She obtained her pilot's licence in 2023, when she was still a 17-year-old high school student in Florida."She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top," Corteleti told The New York Times.Her mother also described her as responsible and hardworking, while saying she was the co-pilot and could not make decisions about the flight.Investigators are yet to establish the precise roles played by the two pilots in the aircraft's final moments or determine what caused the crash. Around 600 nearby residents were displaced following the accident, while one person on the ground suffered a leg injury.
Article Summary: The aircraft was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday when it suddenly went into a steep nosedive. Investigators are examining whether severe weather, ice accumulation and turbulence contributed to the crash. The victims included 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, as well as three other passengers.

Article Title: Prince William apologises after backlash over 3,000-acre Bradninch Estate sale; tenants demand fair valuations, King Charles disappointed as Duchy of Cornwall faces capital gains tax questions
Article Text:
Prince William has apologised following backlash over the planned sale of the 3,000-acre Bradninch Estate in Devon, with King Charles reportedly disappointed by the decision. (Photo: Instagram)

Why Prince William's property sale has sparked backlash

Bradninch Estate tenants are demanding fair property valuations as they consider whether to buy their homes and farms. (Photo: Instagram)

Kensington Palace responds to tenants' concerns

1. The Duchy of Cornwall faces questions over capital gains tax as the estate sale controversy continues. (Photo: Instagram)

Questions raised over tax implications of the sale

Prince William has reportedly apologised to tenants of the Bradninch Estate in Devon following a backlash over his decision to sell the 3,000-acre property, which forms part of the Duchy of Cornwall. The Prince of Wales is said to have been unhappy with reports highlighting residents' concerns about the proposed sale, with some tenants fearing they could lose their homes and livelihoods.According to a report by The Observer, William contacted the Duchy's rural director, Matthew Morris, last Sunday to discuss the growing controversy. Morris subsequently visited the estate on Thursday and met with tenants to address their concerns.During the meeting, the royal representative reportedly apologised for underestimating the time required to complete the land disposal process. He also agreed to arrange fresh independent valuations of the farms and residential properties, with the assessments to be jointly commissioned by the tenants and the Duchy.One tenant described Morris as being "all apologetic", while another reportedly welcomed the conciliatory approach but cautioned that "the proof will be in the pudding".The apology follows growing concerns among residents after the Duchy began the process of selling the Bradninch Estate, a 1,215-hectare (3,000-acre) property in Devon. The estate has been part of the Duchy of Cornwall since the 14th century and represents approximately one-fifth of the land portfolio William inherited from his father, King Charles III, in September 2022.The decision to sell the estate is part of William's wider plan to concentrate future Duchy investment on five geographical heartlands: the Isles of Scilly, Cornwall, Dartmoor, Bath and Kennington in south London.However, the proposed sale has caused considerable anxiety among farming and residential tenants. Last month, possession orders reportedly gave some residents just six months to either purchase their properties or leave.While tenants have been offered the opportunity to buy their homes and farms, some say the valuations are too high and do not adequately account for the money they have invested in improving the properties over the years. Others have raised concerns about their ability to afford the purchases.The controversy has also drawn criticism from Mary Ryan, a former GP who has lived in Bradninch for 36 years and is supporting affected tenants. She has accused William of hypocrisy, arguing that his commitment to tackling homelessness and mental health issues could come at the expense of rural families facing uncertainty over their own homes.Following the backlash, a Kensington Palace spokesperson told The Observer that the concerns surrounding the sale were being taken seriously and that tenants were receiving individual support."We recognise that these are important and deeply personal decisions. Every tenant is being supported through the process on an individual basis, with access to practical guidance from the estate team, independent welfare and mental health support services and ongoing discussions about what is right for their circumstances," the spokesperson said.The statement also explained that the sale was part of a long-term strategy to direct future Duchy of Cornwall investment towards areas where it could deliver greater benefits for communities, farming, nature and the local economy."We will continue to support tenants with care, respect and fairness, whatever decision they ultimately make," the spokesperson added.The Duchy has also said that tenants are being offered the first opportunity to purchase their homes and farms, with discounts taking into account factors such as the length of their tenancy, the type of agreement and investments made in the properties.According to the Duchy, eight out of nine farming tenants are actively exploring the purchase of some or all of their farms, while around two-thirds of residential tenants are considering buying their homes.The proposed disposal has also prompted questions about whether the Duke of Cornwall should pay capital gains tax on the proceeds.A Duchy spokesperson has maintained that the Duke is exempt because proceeds from the disposal of capital assets are required by law to be reinvested and are not available for his personal use.However, tax expert Dan Neidle has challenged that interpretation, arguing that there is no legal basis for such an exemption. He has suggested that if HM Revenue and Customs determines that capital gains tax is payable, the Duke would be required to pay it.The controversy has also reportedly disappointed King Charles, who regularly visited the Bradninch Estate when he was Prince of Wales and regarded it as an example of the rural communities that form the backbone of Britain.For now, the promise of fresh independent valuations has offered some reassurance to tenants. However, residents are still waiting to see whether the Duchy's revised approach will address their concerns over affordability, property improvements and their future on the estate.
Article Summary: Prince William has reportedly apologised to tenants of the Bradninch Estate in Devon following a backlash over his decision to sell the 3,000-acre property. The Prince of Wales is said to have been unhappy with reports highlighting residents' concerns about the proposed sale. The estate has been part of the Duchy of Cornwall since the 14th century and represents approximately one-fifth of the land portfolio William inherited from his father.

Article Title: In 1610, Galileo revealed four moons of Jupiter, but another astronomer called them an illusion; their opposing books survived bound together for centuries before the rare volume sold for Rs 2.07 cror
Article Text:
Galileo, Jupiter and four moons (AI-image)

Rs 2.07 crore book

The little book that changed astronomy

Book at Christie's auction (PC: Christie)

The Starry Messenger

The astronomer who refused to believe

Four books, one volume and centuries of history

Book at Christie's auction (PC: Christie)

From a disputed discovery to an astronomical legacy

Galileo Galilei is a name that needs no introduction. In 1610, Italian astronomer Galileo published a small book that challenged the way people understood the universe. He used a telescope and observed four bodies moving around Jupiter, providing evidence that not everything in the universe revolved around Earth.However, it’s normal that people generally are not convinced with anything that challenges their notion or age-old beliefs. Among those who challenged his findings was astronomer Francesco Sizzi, who argued that the supposed moons were optical illusions produced by the telescope.Now over 400 years later, the books documenting these opposing views have become part of an extraordinary story of scientific discovery.In February 2026, a rare volume containing Galileo’s landmark publication alongside three other early works on astronomy and optics sold at Christie’s for US$217,600, approximately Rs 2.07 crore. It was a collection that was offered as part of the auction house’s sale of fine printed books, manuscripts and science.The book was published in Venice in March 1610. Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius, commonly translated as, announced observations that had become possible through the relatively new technology of the telescope.Galileo learnt about the development of the telescope in 1609 and later built his own improved instruments. By the end of that year, he was using them to observe the night sky. In January 1610, he turned his attention to Jupiter and noticed several points of light near the planet. As he continued observing them on successive nights, their changing positions revealed that they were orbiting Jupiter rather than remaining fixed among the stars.It was a significant discovery as it challenged the established Aristotelian picture of the universe. As per his theory, the heavens were understood through a system of nested celestial spheres and Earth occupied a central position.In Sidereus Nuncius, Galileo also described the Moon’s uneven and mountainous surface. It also mentioned that the Milky Way has numerous individual stars that could not be distinguished with the naked eye.Now this book made Galileo famous across Europe.However, Francesco Sizzi, a contemporary of Galileo, refused to believe his theory and questioned the existence of Jupiter’s newly reported moons.The existence of other bodies orbiting a planet questioned the order in which celestial movements were interpreted. Sizzi argued that the appearances Galileo described could be produced by the telescope itself.The disagreement is particularly intriguing because the two positions survived together in the same physical volume. Sizzi’s Dianoia astronomica, optica, physica, published in Venice in 1611, was bound alongside Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius in the copy later sold by Christie’s.According to Christie’s catalogue, Galileo, in turn, declined to refute Sizzi, preferring to preserve their friendship. The episode offers a glimpse of a time when new scientific observations confronted long-established beliefs, and the debate over evidence was still unfolding.The copy sold in 2026 was more than a first edition of Galileo’s celebrated work. It was a Sammelband, a volume in which separate publications were bound together. Alongside Sidereus Nuncius were three other first editions published in 1611.The second work was Sizzi’s response to the controversy over Jupiter’s moons. The third, by Marcus Antonius de Dominis, explored vision, light, lenses and the rainbow, with material on the telescope added amid the excitement surrounding Galileo’s discoveries. The fourth, by Giovanni Antonio Magini, explored the properties and effects of spherical concave mirrors.According to Christie’s catalogue, the works were bound in contemporary stiff vellum boards. The volume also contains a reused sheet from a 1474 edition of a Latin translation of Herodotus, incorporated into the inside cover. Its binding and surviving details offer a glimpse into how early printed books were assembled and preserved.The four moons Galileo observed are now known as Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.Galileo recorded the changing positions of the points of light over successive nights and recognised that their movement was evidence of their orbit around Jupiter. What initially appeared to be an arrangement of distant stars became evidence that celestial bodies could revolve around a world other than Earth.When the rare volume sold for US$217,600 in 2026, its significance lay in this unusual combination of scientific achievement and intellectual resistance.
Article Summary: A rare volume containing Galileo’s landmark publication alongside three other early works on astronomy and optics sold at Christie's for US$217,600, approximately Rs 2.07 crore. In 1610, Italian astronomer Galileo published a small book that challenged the way people understood the universe. He observed four bodies moving around Jupiter, providing evidence that not everything in the universe revolved around Earth.

Article Title: 'We're out of time': Florida pilot's desperate final warning before private jet plunged to ground, killing 9
Article Text:
'We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,' the co-pilot yelled, 'We’re going to crash into the ground!'

‘Mayday, mayday’: Pilot reports emergency

‘We're descending 10,000 feet per minute’

What happened before the aircraft lost control?

The pilot of the Florida Learjet 60 crash sent out increasingly desperate distress calls moments before the aircraft plunged into a Florida roadway on Sunday, killing all nine people on board. In a chilling final exchange with air traffic controllers, the pilot warned that the aircraft was descending at an extreme speed and cried out, “We’re going to crash into the ground!” CNN reported, citing air traffic control recordings.The aircraft was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida. Its final radio transmissions captured the crew's desperate attempts to communicate the unfolding emergency.According to the report, the pilot had reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius and moderate turbulence shortly before the plane began its rapid descent.The distress calls began at around 12.48 pm ET, when the aircraft was flying over Palm Beach County.According to recordings of air traffic control communications captured by LiveATC.net, the pilot initially reported precipitation and requested permission to climb to 37,000 feet.Air traffic control approved the request.However, seconds later, the pilot declared, “Mayday, mayday!”The aircraft had begun descending rapidly. The pilot first reported a descent rate of 8,000 feet per minute, which soon increased to 10,000 feet per minute.As the situation deteriorated, the pilot informed the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center about the aircraft's rapidly increasing descent rate.“We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!” Filgueiras told the control centre.Moments later, the warning became more urgent.“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” she yelled. “We’re going to crash into the ground!”At 12.49 pm, the pilot reported that the aircraft was falling at 22,000 feet per minute, equivalent to around 367 feet per second.The final transmission came at 12.49.17 pm.“We’re out of time.”Flight-tracking data from ADS-B Exchange showed that the aircraft had plunged around 27,000 feet in approximately one minute before its signal was lost.CNN reported that the pilot had described icing conditions and moderate turbulence shortly before the emergency.The aircraft was flying at approximately 35,000 feet, where temperatures can be extremely low. The pilot reported an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius and described “light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence”.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions were a major focus of its investigation.Icing is a serious aviation hazard. According to the Federal Aviation Administration, ice accumulation can increase an aircraft's weight, reduce lift, decrease thrust and increase drag. It can also make controlling the aircraft's speed and flight path more difficult.The NTSB said investigators were also examining evidence that the aircraft may have broken apart before hitting the ground.The cause of the crash remains under investigation. The NTSB is expected to release a preliminary report within 30 days.
Article Summary: The pilot of the Florida Learjet 60 crash sent out increasingly desperate distress calls moments before the aircraft plunged into a Florida roadway on Sunday, killing all nine people on board. In a chilling final exchange with air traffic controllers, the pilot warned that the aircraft was descending at an extreme speed and cried out, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”

Article Title: In September, inmates at an Ohio jail began drawing portraits of overlooked shelter dogs; two months later, 18 of the 20 dogs featured in the artwork have found homes, giving both animals and artists
Article Text:
Photo credit: Franklin County Dog Shelter in Columbus/ Instagram

The Herbie effect

Humanising the dog shelter

A sense of purpose behind bars

Creative solutions don't need to be complex

If you ever visit a busy animal shelter, you naturally start noticing certain facts like the breed, size, age, how loud a bark is, it all happens subconsciously, and in a matter of seconds. But at the Franklin County Dog Shelter in Columbus, Ohio, visitors walking past the kennels have been stopping for a very different reason: hand-drawn portraits taped right next to the metal doors. Since last autumn, inmates at the Franklin County Corrections Center have been using pencils, paper, and careful observation to sketch dogs waiting for adoption, reported The Washington Post. It is an unlikely partnership between two county institutions that rarely share headlines, but the early numbers tell a striking story. Within roughly two months of launching the initiative, 18 of the first 20 dogs featured in the artwork had already been adopted into permanent homes. Read more about this heart-warming gesture, as reported by The Washington Post, here:Take James Bowshier and his wife as an example. They walked into the shelter with a clear plan in mind: look for a puppy. But as they browsed the runs, a drawing hanging outside one of the kennels caught James’s eye. The portrait showed Herbie, a one-year-old pit bull mix, captured with a level of warmth and detail that made him stand out from the rows of surrounding cages.That single sketch did what standard kennel cards rarely manage to do; it forced the couple to slow down. Instead of sweeping past to look for younger animals, they paused, took a closer look, and asked shelter staff if they could meet Herbie in person.They ended up taking him home that very day. Without that drawing breaking through the noise of the shelter floor, Herbie might easily have been passed over.Shelters are demanding, high-volume environments. Staff members and volunteers work endlessly to manage intakes, medical care, and public visits, but they can only spend so much time introducing each dog to potential adopters. Meanwhile, kennels are inherently loud and stressful. Even the gentlest dog can come across as overly anxious, hyperactive, or completely withdrawn when viewed through wire mesh.Standard kennel tags list crucial information: intake dates, breed estimates, and basic medical history. Valuable as those facts are, they can inadvertently reduce a living animal to an administrative case file. A hand-drawn portrait shifts that dynamic immediately. It tells potential adopters that someone sat down, studied this specific animal's features, and cared enough to translate their personality onto paper. It transforms a quick glance into a moment of genuine human connection.The impact of the project flows both ways. For the artists inside the Franklin County Corrections Center, drawing shelter dogs offers something that can be notoriously hard to find in custody: tangible purpose and a real link to the outside community.Daily life in a correctional facility is heavily structured and offers few opportunities to make a constructive public contribution. Working on these portraits requires patience, steady focus, and hours of quiet concentration. More importantly, it gives participants a chance to create something that actually leaves the facility and serves a clear, positive good. Their work hangs in a public space, helps animals find families, and often ends up framed on the wall of an adopter's living room.No one is claiming that drawing dogs is a cure-all for criminal justice reform or that it solves systemic issues on its own. What it does provide, however, is practical, humane engagement. It allows people in jail to be recognised for their skill and effort rather than solely defined by their current circumstances.It is worth keeping a realistic perspective. A nice drawing cannot replace responsible adoption practices. Bringing a pet into a home requires time, money, proper space, and an honest assessment of whether the animal fits a family's lifestyle. Shelter workers still need to facilitate proper meet-and-greets, discuss behavioral needs, and ensure lasting matches. The artwork simply serves as an invitation; the real work of adoption comes after.Still, what makes this project so compelling is its sheer simplicity. It didn't require high-tech tools, massive funding grants, or complicated administrative overhauls. It just took sketch pads, drawing pencils, cooperation between two local agencies, and a willingness to try something different.By helping prospective adopters see shelter dogs as individuals with stories worth hearing, and by giving incarcerated artists a meaningful way to contribute, a simple sheet of paper has managed to change the trajectory for dozens of lives on both sides of the shelter fence.
Article Summary: Inmates at the Franklin County Corrections Center in Ohio have been drawing dogs waiting for adoption since last autumn. 18 of the first 20 dogs featured in the artwork had already been adopted into permanent homes within two months of launching the initiative. The project is the result of a partnership between two county institutions that rarely share headlines, but the early numbers tell a striking story.

Article Title: Two former partners' fight over a Sausalito house led to a legal-fee demand of $90,010; a California federal judge has now ordered one to pay the other $66,192.50 after a partially successful court mo
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Dispute centred on a Sausalito property

Shroder sought $90,010 in legal expenses

Court reduced the claimed attorney fees

Final award fixed at $66,192.50

A dispute over a shared home can continue long after a relationship ends, particularly when disagreements over property ownership turn into lengthy legal proceedings. In Sausalito, California, a former couple's fight over a house led to a separate dispute over attorney fees after one partner partly succeeded in getting allegations against him struck from a lawsuit. The legal battle took another turn when he sought $90,010 from his former partner to cover his legal expenses. In its October 30, 2026, order in Fotsch v. Shroder, available in Justia, the US District Court for the Northern District of California granted the request in part, ordering Mackenzie Fotsch to pay Matthew Shroder $66,192.50 while rejecting his demand for additional, unspecified fees.Mackenzie Fotsch and Matthew Shroder, who were formerly in a romantic relationship, became involved in litigation concerning a house in Sausalito. Their dispute included an unlawful-detainer action that Shroder had filed and pursued against Fotsch. Fotsch subsequently brought claims against Shroder, including allegations involving contract disputes, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty and conversion. Shroder responded with a special motion to strike under California's anti-SLAPP law.The law protects people from lawsuits targeting their exercise of constitutionally protected rights, including participation in legal proceedings.Shroder argued that certain allegations in Fotsch's complaint relied on his protected litigation activities. The court partly agreed, striking portions of four allegations to the extent that they made his filing, service and prosecution of the unlawful-detainer action a basis for liability. Those allegations could remain in the complaint as background and evidence. However, it refused to dismiss the entire claims and allowed the unjust-enrichment claim to proceed.Following his partial success, Shroder sought attorney fees and costs under California's anti-SLAPP statute, which allows a defendant who prevails on a special motion to strike to recover reasonable legal expenses. His application totalled $90,010. This included $45,685 for the anti-SLAPP motion, $40,720 for preparing and arguing the subsequent attorney-fee motion, and $3,605 in Westlaw legal research charges. He also requested additional fees that might arise later.The application covered work by three lawyers and a paralegal, whose hourly rates ranged from $225 to $900. Fotsch challenged the amount, arguing that Shroder had achieved only limited success because the court had allowed her claims to survive. She also questioned the billing records, the hours claimed and the expenses associated with preparing the fee application. She proposed limiting the award to $3,593, or at most $7,129.50, based on the portions of the anti-SLAPP motion that had succeeded. She also opposed the research charges and the request for unspecified future fees.The judge recognised that Shroder had not secured everything he requested. The court had rejected his attempt to strike entire claims and had allowed the unjust-enrichment claim to continue. However, it found that removing the unlawful-detainer proceedings as a basis for liability and damages had materially narrowed the issues in the lawsuit.Rather than calculating fees solely according to the proportion of allegations struck, the court deducted time associated with unsuccessful portions of the motion. It also removed an hour spent correcting an over-length reply brief. The court consequently approved $40,887.50 in attorney fees for the anti-SLAPP proceedings. It allowed the full $3,605 in Westlaw research expenses, finding that the charges were supported by itemised records and related to the legal issues.The judge separately examined the $40,720 requested for preparing the attorney-fee motion. The work involved 66.8 hours, including 63.4 hours by the principal drafter, nearly twice the 33.9 hours he had spent drafting the original anti-SLAPP motion. The court considered this excessive. It also noted that parts of the application repeated arguments already decided and included discussions of the lawyers' professional backgrounds and criticism of opposing counsel. The court therefore reduced the principal lawyer's claimed time by 50 per cent, bringing the recoverable fees for the fee application to $21,700.The court ordered Fotsch to pay Shroder $62,587.50 in attorney fees, comprising $40,887.50 for the anti-SLAPP proceedings and $21,700 for the fee application. An additional $3,605 was allowed for legal research costs. The judge rejected Shroder's request for further, unquantified attorney fees, requiring any additional expenses to be specified and supported. The October 30 order resolves the attorney-fee dispute, not the underlying disagreement over the Sausalito property. Fotsch's remaining claims were not dismissed, and the ruling does not determine the ultimate outcome of the former partners' wider legal battle.
Article Summary: Mackenzie Fotsch and Matthew Shroder became involved in litigation concerning a house in Sausalito, California. Their dispute included an unlawful-detainer action that Shoder had filed and pursued against Fotch. FotsCh subsequently brought claims against ShoDer, including allegations involving contract disputes, unjust enrichment, breach of fiduciary duty and conversion. ShroDer responded with a special motion to strike under California's anti-SLAPP law. The court partly agreed, striking portions of four allegations to the extent that they made his filing, service and prosecution a basis for liability.

Article Title: In Oklahoma, discarded dumpsters have been transformed into Hazmatt, a 20-foot-tall reclining robot holding a wildflower; the city spent just over $14,000 on the public artwork unveiled in January 202
Article Text:
A giant robot built from discarded waste

How much did the city spend on Hazmatt?

Why the robot stands at a hazardous waste facility

What happens when discarded dumpsters are given a second life? In Norman, Oklahoma, they have been turned into a 20-foot-tall robot that reclines on a hillside, holding a wildflower in one hand. Called Hazmatt, the unusual public sculpture transforms retired waste containers and reclaimed materials into an artwork designed to encourage people to rethink their relationship with rubbish and the environment. The City of Norman funded the multi-year project with just over $14,000 from leftover construction funds, and the sculpture was officially unveiled in January 2026.According to an announcement by the City of Norman dated December 12, 2025, Hazmatt was created by Kenneth Eugene Hall Jr., a Norman-based artist and founding member of Crucible Art Foundry and Gallery. The sculpture stands at the city's Household Hazardous Waste Facility, where it serves as a reminder that materials often treated as waste can still have a purpose.Unlike conventional public sculptures made from bronze, stone or steel, Hazmatt was constructed almost entirely from retired dumpsters and reclaimed waste materials.The project brought together the idea of recycling with an imaginative design, turning objects associated with rubbish collection into a giant figure with a distinctly relaxed appearance. Hazmatt's reclining posture is central to its message. Rather than depicting a robot in an aggressive stance or dramatic action pose, the sculpture appears to be resting on the hillside, holding a wildflower. The contrast between the imposing size of the figure and the delicate flower gives the installation a gentler character.The city describes Hazmatt as a “gentle giant”, with its relaxed and contemplative posture intended to encourage residents to consider their connection with the environment. Its construction also demonstrates how discarded materials can be repurposed rather than sent directly for disposal. Roadside America, which documented the installation following its unveiling, identifies local artists Ken Hall Jr. and Derek Vosten in connection with the sculpture. The travel website describes Hazmatt as being assembled from dozens of old dumpsters. The city's original announcement, however, names Hall Jr. as the sculpture's creator.The sculpture's reported cost is another notable aspect of the project. The City of Norman said the multi-year undertaking was funded at just over $14,000, using leftover construction funds from its Household Hazardous Waste Facility Capital Project. The city used money remaining from the facility's construction project to support an installation that also reflects the site's environmental purpose. The city said all fabrication and assembly took place either at the facility itself or at the city's Container Maintenance Facility. This connected the sculpture's creation to the municipal operations that handle waste and maintain city equipment.Hazmatt was officially dedicated during a ribbon-cutting ceremony on January 13, 2026, at 3803 Chautauqua Avenue. A subsequent report by Hoodline said the event included remarks from Mayor Stephen Tyler Holman, City Manager Darrel Pyle, artist Ken Hall Jr. and Derek Vosten, among others. The city's council meeting records also refer to the ribbon-cutting and describe the sculpture as a creative, cost-effective alternative to disposing of decommissioned dumpsters.The sculpture stands at Norman's Household Hazardous Waste Facility, which began operating in 2022 and provides residents with a place to dispose of or recycle materials that require special handling. According to the city, the facility accepts items including pesticides, kerosene and paint removers. Such products cannot always be treated like ordinary household rubbish, making appropriate collection and disposal important for environmental protection.By placing the sculpture at the facility, the city has connected a public artwork with a practical waste-management service. Visitors arriving to dispose of household hazardous materials encounter a giant figure built from discarded objects, reinforcing the idea that responsible waste handling begins with considering what happens to unwanted materials.Michele Loudenback, manager of the city's Division of Environmental Resilience and Sustainability, said Hazmatt would act as a friendly ambassador for visitors to the facility. In the city's announcement, she described the installation as an example of waste reduction and resourcefulness. The sculpture's message is therefore not limited to recycling alone. Its design encourages people to think about how everyday decisions, including the disposal of potentially harmful products, affect the environment.
Article Summary: The City of Norman funded the multi-year project with just over $14,000 from leftover construction funds, and the sculpture was officially unveiled in January 2026. The sculpture stands at the city's Household Hazardous Waste Facility, where it serves as a reminder that materials often treated as waste can still have a purpose.

Article Title: In 1968, Canadian Club hid whisky behind Venezuela’s Angel Falls; newlyweds found the case after a jungle trek, one of 25 stashed worldwide
Article Text:
Canadian Club’s Hide A Case promotion, launched in 1967, hid cases of whiskey in remote locations. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Canadian Club hid its second whiskey case at Angel Falls in 1968

Mickeys, Minis and Punts: An Investigation of the Marketing and Advertising Initiatives of Seagram and Hiram Walker, 1950-1969

David and Diana Mattoon changed their honeymoon plans to find the whiskey

Canadian Club hid 25 whiskey cases between 1967 and 1991

Angel Falls, Venezuela. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Canadian Club revived the treasure hunt in 2010

In 1968, newlyweds David and Diana Mattoon had a very different kind of honeymoon. The newlyweds changed their planned trip to Acapulco and travelled to Venezuela to search for a hidden case of Canadian Club whiskey. Their journey took them into the rainforest near Angel Falls, where they found one of the cases placed around the world as part of an unusual advertising campaign.The Hide a Case campaign by Canadian Club started in 1967, when it was under the ownership of Hiram Walker. In this marketing strategy, the firm used to hide cases of Canadian Club and then gave hints to the same, which could be found through advertisements in magazines. According to Rochelle Pereira-Alvares’s thesis,, archived at Library and Archives Canada , the campaign launched in July 1967, with the first case hidden in Tanzania, close to Mount Kilimanjaro. A second case was hidden at Angel Falls in Venezuela in January 1968. A contemporary report published in The Washington Post on 26 August 1979, by Joseph P. Mastrangelo, titled Whiskey in the Wild, describes the early campaign and what was discovered by two honeymooners, David and Diana Mattoon.The couple had earlier planned on having their honeymoon in Acapulco, Mexico.Diana believed they were headed to Acapulco until David revealed his real plan while they were still in the air: to travel to Venezuela and search for the Canadian Club case near Angel Falls. The newlyweds travelled through the rainforest in difficult conditions, encountering heavy rain and mosquitoes along the way.
