David and Diana were also added to the search by a guide who was called Jungle Rudy. Mastrangelo’s 1979 article says Rudy had earlier helped the advertising team hide the whiskey case. David and Diana found the case within days of starting their trek into the rainforest, according to Mastrangelo’s report.The search for the Angel Falls case was just one component of a broad promotion that hid cases of Canadian Club in unexpected places worldwide. Between 1967 and 1991, Canadian Club hid 25 whiskey cases in remote locations around the world, according to VinePair’s article “The Long History of Canadian Club’s ‘Hide a Case’ Campaign.” These hidden cases were found at Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, Angel Falls in Venezuela, the Swiss Alps, the Arctic Circle and Death Valley in California. There were also cases found close to the Great Barrier Reef in Australia and on top of a skyscraper in Manhattan.In an announcement by Canadian Club’s parent Company, Beam Global Spirits & Wine, dated May 17, 2010, it is stated that 16 of the 25 cases had been found by them. The company also said that clues published in their print advertisement in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s aided many people in finding the cases. Canadian Club revived it at different times, allowing people another chance at following the clues.Hide a Case was revived in May 2010 by Canadian Club and participants in Canada and the United States were challenged to enter a contest with an opportunity to join an expedition around the globe to discover one of the hidden cases and receive a $100,000 reward. As mentioned in the company's press release, World-Famous Treasure Hunt Resurrected, the contest included such challenges as online contests, video submissions and treasure hunting. Four Canadians and four Americans were to be chosen to join an expedition led by television personality Kevin Brauch.The chosen participants were to meet at a secret destination in April 2011 and complete several challenges to uncover the mystery of the lost case. As a result, the old promotion regained popularity through online participation alongside the original search for hidden whiskey. The Mattoons’ honeymoon search for whiskey at Angel Falls, in the Venezuelan rainforest, was among the campaign’s most notable episodes.
Article Summary: The Hide a Case campaign by Canadian Club started in 1967, when it was under the ownership of Hiram Walker. Between 1967 and 1991, Canadian Club hid 25 whiskey cases in remote locations around the world. These cases were found at Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, Angel Falls in Venezuela, the Swiss Alps, the Arctic Circle and Death Valley in California.

Article Title: In 2006, Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter started a mentoring programme with just eight or nine girls; 20 years later, it has involved around 1,500 young women and more than 1,000 volunteer mento
Article Text:
Judge Judy Sheindlin (right) and her daughter Nicole Sheindlin (left)Photo: Her honor nation/ Instagram

How the programme began

Who Her Honor serves

What mentors actually do

Why the model works

A network, not just a programme

Twenty years of second chances

When Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter Nicole Sheindlin launched Her Honor Mentoring in 2006, it began with a modest group of eight or nine high-school girls and a simple belief: a trusted professional woman could help a young person see a wider future for herself. Twenty years later, the programme has grown into a regional mentoring network involving approximately 1,500 mentees and more than 1,000 volunteer mentors, according to Fox News and Her Honor Mentoring.The programme’s growth is impressive, but its purpose has remained remarkably consistent. Her Honor connects motivated high-school senior girls, many of whom are first-generation college-bound students from families with limited financial resources, with mentors who can offer practical guidance on education, careers, confidence and money. What began as a small experiment has become a structured nine-month experience designed to open doors that might otherwise remain closed.Nicole Sheindlin has described the programme as a reflection of her own relationship with Judge Judy. After attending the same law school as her stepmother, she later sat beside her in family court, where she saw the influence a strong professional woman could have on a young person’s outlook and opportunities.That experience became the model for Her Honor.The idea was not simply to give girls advice. It was to create sustained relationships between young women and mentors from different professional worlds, allowing mentees to ask questions, test ambitions and learn how to navigate education and work. Judge Judy and Nicole concluded that they could help young women gain extra skills and expand their professional networks by building a programme around that kind of connection.The first class was tiny. Judge Judy recalled that it included only eight or nine participants, while the most recent class in September had more than 100. That growth did not happen overnight, but it shows how a small, well-designed programme can scale when schools, businesses and volunteers see its value.Her Honor works with high-school senior girls nominated by their schools. The organisation says its mentees are first-generation, college-bound students from families with limited financial resources, a focus that places the programme where mentorship and professional networks can make the greatest difference.Participants are not left to work things out alone. Her Honor pairs mentors and mentees carefully, taking into account interests and life experiences in order to build relationships based on trust and relevance. The programme’s stated aim is to create a productive and inspiring mentoring relationship rather than a one-off meeting or a generic career talk.The programme now operates across the Bronx, Westchester and Rockland counties in New York, with a pilot initiative in Burlington, New Jersey. Its growth from eight students at one high school to more than 100 students across multiple schools reflects both rising demand and the involvement of local schools, businesses and community organisations.The core of Her Honor is a nine-month hybrid mentoring experience focused on college and career readiness. Mentoring teams meet weekly throughout the academic year, guided by the Her Honor curriculum and arranged at times and places that fit busy schedules.The curriculum goes beyond academic achievement. Mentees work on communication, problem-solving, time management and accountability, while also receiving support around college applications, career exploration and professional presentation. In practice, that can mean learning how to write an email, prepare for an interview, manage deadlines or think seriously about life after high school.Financial literacy is another central part of the experience. Judge Judy told Fox News that participants are paid for working and learn how to dress for success, make first impressions, manage money and become financially prepared for adulthood. The combination of practical work, mentoring and financial education is intended to give young women tools they can use long after the programme ends.Mentorship often succeeds because it gives young people access to knowledge that is not always available at home or school. A mentor can explain how a workplace operates, what college life is really like, how to handle setbacks or how to ask for help without feeling embarrassed. Those conversations can change how a student imagines her own future.Her Honor also recognises that confidence is practical, not abstract. Former mentee Keiry Alvarez said the programme helped her overcome timidity, while her mentor Lilliana Mendoza said Her Honor helped her gain people skills, find her voice and receive guidance that influenced her career as a police officer. These personal accounts show how the programme’s structure translates into everyday confidence.The programme’s impact extends to mentors as well. Nicole Sheindlin said mentors have discovered that giving back supports their own wellbeing, while Judge Judy noted that several former mentees have returned as mentors after beginning their careers. That cycle turns a mentoring programme into a community habit, where each generation helps prepare the next.One of Her Honor’s strengths is the breadth of its volunteer base. Fox News reported that more than 1,000 mentors have taken part from 400 organisations and businesses over the programme’s 20-year history. That range exposes mentees to careers and professional environments they may not otherwise encounter.The organisation describes mentoring as a way to bridge education gaps with local business resources. Its philosophy is that investing in young people is essential to building healthy, equitable and resilient communities, and the involvement of companies and professionals gives that philosophy practical form.The current 2026 to 2027 class includes 108 mentees and 123 mentors across 14 schools in the Bronx, Rockland and Westchester counties. The fact that mentors slightly outnumber mentees reflects the programme’s team-based approach, in which guidance is shared rather than delivered by a single adult.Judge Judy has spent much of her public life dealing with conflict, dysfunction and difficult decisions. Her Honor offers a different kind of legacy, one built on prevention, encouragement and practical opportunity. She told Fox News that seeing young women still hoping, dreaming and working hard renews her faith in people.The programme’s numbers tell one part of the story: 1,500 mentees, more than 1,000 mentors and 31 high schools involved over two decades. But its deeper achievement may be quieter. It has helped young women develop the confidence, skills and relationships needed to pursue education and work with greater purpose.Her Honor began with a handful of girls and a mother-daughter partnership. Two decades later, it has become proof that mentorship, when done consistently and thoughtfully, can create a cycle of opportunity that reaches far beyond its first classroom.
Article Summary: Judge Judy Sheindlin and her daughter Nicole started Her Honor Mentoring in 2006. The programme has grown into a regional mentoring network involving 1,500 mentees and more than 1,000 volunteer mentors. Her Honor connects motivated high-school senior girls with mentors who can offer practical guidance on education, careers, confidence and money.

Article Title: A divorced mother with no restaurant experience, Ruth Fertel mortgaged her New Orleans home in 1965 to buy a 60-seat steakhouse; it became Ruth’s Chris
Article Text:
Ruth's Chris Steak House. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The purchase on North Broad Street

A dining room run by single mothers

From two restaurants to a global chain

Rear and side view of the building that formerly housed Ruth’s Chris House at 711 North Broad Street, New Orleans. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why the gamble worked

After her marriage ended in 1958, Ruth Fertel supported her two young sons on her own and later spent four years working at Tulane University Medical School, according to the Horatio Alger Association. In 1965, she purchased Chris Steak House, the restaurant that later became Ruth’s Chris Steak House, the Horatio Alger Association noted. Her salary was not enough to send her sons to college, so she began looking for a way to earn more. Then she noticed an advertisement for a restaurant for sale near the racetrack in New Orleans.She had no restaurant experience and her banker, lawyer, family and friends all advised her not to go ahead, according to the company‘s own history. But she went ahead and bought it, risking her home and turning a little steakhouse on North Broad Street into a household name.Entrepreneur Chris Matulich founded Chris Steak House in New Orleans in 1927 and operated it at 1100 North Broad Street, according to Ruth’s Chris Steak House. In 1965, Ruth Fertel spotted a classified ad for Chris Steak House in the newspaper while looking for a way to pay for her two sons’ education.Despite having no restaurant experience, she mortgaged her home for $22,000, using $18,000 to buy the 60-seat restaurant and the remaining $4,000 for food and supplies, according to Ruth’s Chris Steak House. The restaurant was small. It could accommodate only 60 customers, had no parking and stood near the Fair Grounds Race Course. The area was crowded and the restaurant was struggling even before she took it over. Hurricane Betsy hit New Orleans in September 1965, the same year she bought the restaurant.On her first day as owner, Fertel reportedly sold 35 steaks at around $5 each, Mashed reported, citing an archived biography. The dining room was staffed entirely by hard-working, single mothers who later became known as the “Broads on Broad Street", according to the official Ruth’s Chris Steak House website. For many years, it was the only upscale restaurant in New Orleans with an all-female wait staff. In early 1976, shortly after Ruth Fertel signed a new 10-year lease, a kitchen fire destroyed the original Chris Steak House, forcing her to move to a nearby property on Broad Street. Until then, the restaurant had operated under its original name for 11 years. A businessman working in construction agreed to help her and she moved into a bigger restaurant with 160 seats, up from the original 60.Under her contract with Matulich, Fertel could not use the Chris Steak House Name at any other location. So she added her own name in front of the original, creating Ruth’s Chris Steak House. She told Fortune in 1998 that she had always hated the name, but had learnt to live with it, Mental Floss reported.Fertel worked hard at her New Orleans restaurant and never thought of taking the business beyond the city limits. That changed when a loyal customer who had moved to Baton Rouge kept travelling back to New Orleans for dinner, which prompted her to start franchising, according to Encyclopedia.com.In 1999, Fertel sold a majority stake in the company to Madison Dearborn Partners but kept a minority share. She died in 2002. The firm now has over 150 outlets in operation globally.The restaurant's success came from practical decisions, including the loyal staff, consistent service and stubborn determination to start again after the fire. The little 60-seat steakhouse on North Broad Street has since grown into a worldwide name and the brand still carries the name she was forced to add.
Article Summary: Ruth Fertel bought Chris Steak House in 1965 while looking for a way to pay for her two sons' education. She mortgaged her home for $22,000, using $18,000 to buy the 60-seat restaurant and the remaining $4,000 for food and supplies. The dining room was staffed entirely by hard-working, single mothers who later became known as the “Broads on Broad Street’ For many years, it was the only upscale restaurant in New Orleans with an all-female wait staff.

Article Title: A Wisconsin father gave his son a stake in the family car dealership, but a feud over ownership and company money lasted more than a decade; an appeals court upheld $321,330 in civil-theft damages aga
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How a family dealership became the subject of an ownership dispute

Company money used to settle personal obligations

Court finds three instances of civil theft

Seventh Circuit rejects son's arguments

A family business can become the centre of a bitter dispute when questions over ownership, financial decisions and control begin to divide relatives. In Wisconsin, a disagreement between a father and son over a family-owned car dealership continued for more than a decade, eventually leading to multiple lawsuits, allegations of misuse of company funds and a court-ordered dissolution of the business. What began as a family ownership arrangement ultimately resulted in the son being held personally liable for civil theft.In its October 30, 2026, decision in Carl Schneider v. Chris Schneider, available on Justia, the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit upheld a judgment against Chris Schneider, rejecting his challenge to $321,330 in exemplary damages awarded for three instances of civil theft. The appeals court found no clear error in the lower court's conclusion that he had knowingly used company money for purposes he was not authorised to pursue. The ruling also addressed his argument that an earlier lawsuit prevented the trust from seeking certain damages again.The dispute centred on Hybrid Car Store Inc., a car dealership in La Crosse, Wisconsin, founded by Carl Schneider in 1976. His son, Chris, became the company's general manager about a decade later. Carl initially gave Chris a 25% ownership stake, while Carl and his wife, Narcelle, each retained 37.5%.The family later established the Carl and Narcelle Schneider Trust as part of their estate planning, transferring their respective ownership interests into it. This gave the trust a 75% stake in the company.The situation changed in 2008 when Narcelle transferred her 37.5% interest from the trust to Chris, making him the majority shareholder with 62.5% ownership. Carl challenged the transfer in state court in 2014, arguing that it violated the estate arrangements and that Chris had breached his fiduciary duties. The state court ruled that the transfer violated certain agreements and ordered Chris to pay $562,500 for the ownership interest he had improperly received. It also directed him to pay the trust $56,250 in withheld dividends, along with interest.According to the Seventh Circuit's account of the case, Chris subsequently arranged for the company to provide him with a loan of $281,196.61 and a dividend payment of $281,303.39 to help satisfy the state-court judgment. He then used company-issued payments to pay the amounts owed to the trust. The dispute continued when the company later indemnified Chris for $395,574.81 in legal expenses from the earlier state-court proceedings. He used the money to repay the company loan and took the remaining amount in cash. However, Chris did not repay the company the $56,250 drawn from its account.Another disagreement arose over the dealership's property expenses. The company had repaved its parking lot and replaced its roof in 2012. Carl alleged that Chris improperly attributed those expenses to him personally rather than to the company. In 2018, Chris negotiated the sale of the dealership to Dahl Automotive. During the negotiations, he arranged a monthly rent subsidy of $15,000 for Dahl without informing the trust. After the dealership was sold in March 2019, the company was made to pay these subsidies. The trust also alleged that Chris failed to distribute the dealership sale proceeds to the shareholders.Carl and his daughter, Mary Schneider, acting as trustees, filed the federal lawsuit in December 2019. They accused Chris of improperly obtaining company loans, breaching his fiduciary duties and committing civil theft. After reviewing the evidence and conducting a bench trial, the US District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin found Chris liable for several financial irregularities.The court identified three instances of civil theft: using $56,250 in company funds to satisfy his personal state-court judgment, directing the company to pay $191,500 in rent subsidies promised to Dahl Automotive, and using a dividend intended for the trust to cover a disputed promissory note created in 2021. The court found that Chris had arranged for a promissory note to be created in Carl's name for the earlier roof and parking lot expenses, despite Carl having no knowledge of it. The arrangement allowed Chris to use the trust's share of a company dividend to cover the disputed promissory note, while receiving a corresponding dividend himself.Under Wisconsin law, civil theft can result in exemplary damages when the required elements of theft are established. The district court awarded the trust $321,330 in exemplary damages for the three incidents. It also ordered the company to pay the trust $553,905.49, directed the company's dissolution and appointed a receiver to oversee its affairs.Chris challenged the findings, arguing that he believed he had authority to make the payments and had attempted to repay the money. He also maintained that an earlier federal lawsuit involving the dealership's roof and parking lot expenses prevented the trust from pursuing related damages again. The Seventh Circuit rejected both arguments. The appeals court explained that the 2021 promissory note and the subsequent dividend arrangement involved new actions that occurred years after the earlier litigation. Therefore, the previous case did not prevent the trust from pursuing claims arising from those later events.On the civil-theft findings, the court agreed that Chris knew the company was not responsible for his personal judgment or the rent subsidies he had promised Dahl. It also found sufficient evidence that he knew he lacked authority to use company funds through the disputed promissory note arrangement. The court further clarified that an intention to repay money later does not provide a defence to theft under the relevant Wisconsin statute.The appeals court declined to review the separate damages judgment against the company because Chris lacked standing to challenge it. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the amended judgment against Chris Schneider and remanded the case for the limited purpose of determining the trust's attorney fees and costs incurred during the appeal. The ruling was issued as a nonprecedential disposition, meaning it is not binding precedent in other cases.
Article Summary: The dispute centred on Hybrid Car Store Inc., a car dealership in La Crosse, Wisconsin, founded by Carl Schneider in 1976. His son, Chris, became the company's general manager about a decade later. Carl initially gave Chris a 25% ownership stake, while Carl and his wife, Narcelle, each retained 37.5%. The family later established the Carl andNarcelle Schneider Trust as part of their estate planning, transferring their respective ownership interests into it. This gave the trust a 75% stake in the company.

Article Title: A Colorado landowner protected more than 7,400 acres from future development in 2025; the vast ranch remains home to elk, bears and river otters
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image of a vast canyon ranch, featuring rugged cliffs, forested slopes and a winding river. Image credits: ChatGPT

Why this 7,400-acre ranch is important for wildlife

How a conservation easement protects land without completely

ending ranching

Crested Butte from the North Fork Valley in Gunnison County, Colorado. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The landowner’s long-term vision for the ranch

In western Colorado, a huge working ranch has received permanent protection from future development. This move has safeguarded the landscape in which agriculture, wildlife and river ecosystems all coexist. The Colorado West Land Trust , in February 2025, announced that owner Peter Slaugh had entered into a partnership with the organisation to conserve Scenic Mesa Ranch, which is a 7,419-acre estate located south of Hotchkiss in the North Fork Valley. Situated close to the confluence of two major waterways, the ranch contains extensive river corridors, canyons, grazing land and wildlife habitats. Therefore, the property’s agricultural legacy and ecological importance are protected by the easement while also allowing permitted ranching activities to continue.The location of the Scenic Mesa Ranch is considered strategically important as it is located south of Hotchkiss, stretching along the river corridors upstream from the meeting junction of the North Fork of the Gunnison River and the mainstem of the Gunnison River. According to the Colorado West Land Trust, the region also helps connect lower-elevation public lands with the West Elk Wilderness.The ranch is adjacent to more than 13,000 acres of already conserved land. This conservation easement, therefore, adds to an existing network of protected landscapes.On the other hand, the landscape’s ecological value comes from the variety of environments contained within the boundaries. The vegetated zones alongside rivers and streams fall under its riparian areas and provide habitat for aquatic wildlife and water-dependent bird species. The organisation identifies bald eagles, golden eagles, river otters, elk, mule deer, bighorn sheep, mountain lions and black bears among animals associated with the estate. In addition to that, the ranch contains winter range that elk use, providing forage and cover during colder months. Protecting these various habitats within one estate helps retain the environmental conditions and connections on which wildlife depends.Through a conservation easement, the protection of Scenic Mesa Ranch was achieved. In other words, this was a voluntary legal agreement that allows a landowner to retain private ownership while permanently restricting specified development rights. Under this agreement, the Colorado West Land Trust holds the easement and is responsible for enforcing its terms. Usually, these restrictions prevent prohibited subdivision and development, although the exact conditions depend on the individual agreement. In an interview with KVNF in April 2025, the organisation’s conservation director Ilana Moir explained that the arrangement allows land to remain privately owned while also preserving its values.This distinction is important at Scenic Mesa Ranch because the estate continues to support agricultural production. As per the original conservation arrangement, its existing uses include livestock grazing, irrigated hay production and dryland pastures. Furthermore, the agreement permanently secures the ranch’s senior water rights. This helps protect the legal water resources linked to its continued agricultural use. Slaugh, in a statement, shed light on the importance of water in Colorado’s dry climate, explaining that it plays a key role in maintaining healthy habitats.Slaugh’s decision to establish the easement was also influenced by his thinking about the future of the property. In an interview with KVNF’s Local Motion on April 15, 2025, he mentioned that he was born in Pennsylvania and spent most of his adulthood in California’s Bay Area and the Tahoe region before moving to western Colorado. He had not originally come to the North Fork Valley to raise cattle or grow crops; instead, he was drawn to the landscapes.One of Slaugh’s concerns was whether his children would be able to retain the entire property eventually. He reportedly said that establishing the conservation easement helped resolve such questions regarding the ranch’s long-term future, as the agreement provides a way to protect the landscape’s conservation values even if it sees a change in ownership in coming years.The next steps for the Scenic Mesa conservation effort will involve improving the conditions of the natural habitats. The organisation, along with Slaugh, reportedly plans to collaborate on aquatic and upland restoration projects, such as river restoration work with the Western Colorado Conservation Corps. The broader restoration effort is also expected to address invasive species and riparian corridors.
Article Summary: Scenic Mesa Ranch is a 7,419-acre estate located south of Hotchkiss in the North Fork Valley. Situated close to the confluence of two major waterways, the ranch contains extensive river corridors, canyons, grazing land and wildlife habitats. The ranch is adjacent to more than 13,000 acres of already conserved land. This conservation easement adds to an existing network of protected landscapes.

Article Title: 'America taking its place': Shehbaz's rival Fazlur Rehman accuses Asim Munir of sabotaging ties with China
Article Text: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Monday accused Pakistan army of derailing Chinese investments under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor ( CPEC ), alleging that the country's mineral wealth was being used to advance foreign interests and facilitate a shift towards United States.In a social media post on X, Rehman claimed that Pakistan had disappointed Beijing by halting CPEC-linked investments midway and warned that the loss of Chinese confidence could deter other countries from investing in Pakistan."You have disappointed China, you have halted their investment midway, and when China is disappointed, the rest of the world will not come to invest in your country either," he saidHe alleged that the US was stepping in to fill the space left by China, claiming that American officials had acknowledged this to him."And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me," he said.Rehman clarified that he was not opposed to foreign investment in Pakistan's mineral sector, saying the country urgently needed international capital, development projects and economic opportunities."We do not disagree with the principle of investment from around the world here.Multinational companies come, they invest; America is not immune to this, Russia is not immune, China is not immune, Britain and France are not immune," he said."And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me, and our esteemed elders here have taken those beautiful, beautiful stones to their offices and presented them, and the ambassador they have here at the time has also said it in her interview," he added.The JUI-F chief also alleged that politicians backed by the military establishment prioritised their personal interests and the demands of their patrons over Pakistan's economic well-being."These Pakistani politicians - whose priorities I know - in all such matters, they first determine their own share, and only then do they think about the country," he said.Fazlur Rehman also questioned the imposition of governor's rule and the declaration of an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, alleging that the measures were linked to concerns over the region's mineral reserves."On what grounds? Terrorism? The provincial government is aligned with the narrative of terrorism; it is the federation that is not providing support for that narrative," he said.He further alleged that the focus on terrorism had subsequently disappeared from the debate, while discussions surrounding mineral reserves had also been dropped."As soon as governor's rule was imposed and as soon as the emergency was declared, the topic of terrorism simply vanished, and from their side, the discussion of mineral reserves was dropped," he said.His remarks come amid Pakistan's efforts to attract foreign investment into its mineral sector, particularly in resource-rich regions such as Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.CPEC, a flagship component of China's Belt and Road Initiative, includes infrastructure, energy and industrial development projects. The initiative has faced challenges over the years, including security threats, delays and concerns over the safety of Chinese personnel and investments.
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Monday accused Pakistan army of derailing Chinese investments under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor ( CPEC ), alleging that the country's mineral wealth was being used to advance foreign interests. He warned that the loss of Chinese confidence could deter other countries from investing in Pakistan.

Article Title: Pakistan's confidence crisis: Government officials plan to move families abroad for secure future
Article Text:
Shehbaz Sharif-led Pakistan govt faces confidence crisis as officials plan to move families abroad.

Pakistan is facing questions over the confidence of its own governing establishment, with defence minister Khawaja Asif alleging that some officials holding important positions in the country are planning to settle abroad, including in Portugal and other Western nations.The reported plans have drawn attention to a wider contradiction for the nation grappled with the economic crisis.While the government expects citizens to remain patient amid the country's difficulties, some people within the administration are said to be looking at opportunities and a more secure future overseas for themselves and their families, reported Greek City Times.The issue goes beyond officials moving abroad after retirement as it also raises questions about whether their families are already preparing to build lives elsewhere through overseas education, residency and eventual settlement.If the children of officials study and settle abroad, their families could become less dependent on Pakistan's institutions, even as those officials continue to hold positions of authority at home.The issue of family members studying abroad is also covered in Pakistan's official disclosure requirements. The Establishment Division's asset declaration form asks government officials to provide details of their children's education, including whether they are studying in Pakistan or overseas.It also seeks information about relevant family assets and expenditure.These requirements do not establish how many officials have sent their children abroad or whether they intend to settle overseas. However, they show that such financial arrangements are considered relevant to official disclosure and scrutiny.The reported plans come against the backdrop of a wider migration trend involving Pakistan's educated and professional workforce.In October, overseas Pakistanis minister Chaudhry Salik Hussain told the National Assembly that more than 1.8 million highly educated and professional people had left Pakistan over the previous three years, Pakistan Today reported.The people who moved abroad included doctors, information technology professionals, engineers, academics and skilled workers from several other sectors. Their departure raises concerns about the country's ability to retain experienced professionals across essential industries.The figures cited by the minister underline the scale of the movement of skilled workers out of Pakistan at a time of unprecendented economic crisis.
Article Summary: Pakistan facing confidence crisis as officials plan to move families abroad. Defence minister Khawaja Asif alleges some officials are planning to settle abroad, including in Portugal and other Western nations. Issue goes beyond officials moving abroad after retirement as it also raises questions about whether their families are already preparing to build lives elsewhere.

Article Title: Pakistan gas crisis: Families return to firewood as LPG prices soar ahead of winter
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan's fuel crisis forces families back to firewood and coal

With natural gas available for barely six hours a day and LPG prices soaring, families in Pakistan’s Rawalpindi are returning to firewood, coal and kerosene to keep their kitchens running as winter approaches.According to a report by The Express Tribune, households are increasingly relying on cheaper alternatives such as discarded furniture wood and sawdust. Residents are also facing steep increases in the cost of LPG cylinders, with a new domestic cylinder selling for PKR13,500 (approx Rs 4644), compared with PKR10,000 (approx Rs 3440) earlier. Refill charges have risen from PKR3,000 (approx Rs 1032) to PKR5,000 (approx Rs 1720), while commercial cylinder refills have nearly doubled to PKR25,000 (approx Rs 8600).The cost of firewood and coal has also climbed. Dry firewood is selling for PKR1,500 (approx Rs 516) to PKR1,800 (approx Rs 619) per maund, while ordinary firewood costs PKR1,300 (approx 447) to PKR1,400 (approx Rs 482). Coal is priced between PKR800 (approx Rs 275) and PKR1,000 (approx Rs 344) per maund, depending on quality, and sawdust costs around PKR700 (approx Rs 240) per maund.Muhammad Faizan, a furniture factory owner, told The Express Tribune that waste wood previously dumped near Nullah Lai was now being collected by residents for cooking.Shehzad Manzoor Kiyani, divisional president of the All-Pakistan Clerks Association, said inflation and unreliable gas supplies had forced government employees to return to firewood and coal. He said households were spending PKR10,000 (approx Rs 3440) to PKR12,000 (approx Rs 4127) a month on LPG.The household crisis comes as Pakistan’s LPG supply faces further pressure. The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) has raised the official LPG price for November to PKR 294,075 (approx Rs 1,01,138) per tonne, from PKR 279,341 (approx Rs 96,084) in October. The price of an 11.8-kg domestic cylinder has consequently risen by PKR 173 (approx Rs 59) to PKR 3,470 (approx Rs 1,194), taking the official retail rate to PKR 294 (approx Rs 101) per kg.But LPG is reportedly selling for as much as PKR 630 (approx Rs 217) per kg in the open market, while company-operated franchises are charging up to PKR 400 (approx Rs 138) per kg. Ogra said the increase followed a 6.47% rise in Saudi Aramco’s contract price, despite a marginal 0.12% decline in the average dollar exchange rate.LPG Distributors Association of Pakistan chairman Irfan Khokhar said the situation was serious because of the closure of the Iran border. He claimed that at least 70% of Pakistan’s LPG was imported from Iran, with the remaining 30% produced locally, and urged the government to curb market manipulation.Meanwhile, the Pakistan LPG Marketers Association has threatened to shut down businesses from November 16 if the government sidelines the private sector under its proposed LPG policy. Association chairman Ali Haider said the government should retain the sector’s deregulated structure, arguing that the private sector played a major role in imports.Haider said that of around 1.3 million tonnes of LPG consumed, approximately 225,000 tonnes were imported from the Gulf, largely by private companies. In a letter to petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, the association said the draft policy sent to the prime minister had been prepared without private-sector input and called for complete deregulation of the LPG sector.The association also criticised the petroleum development levy of Rs4,669 per tonne on locally produced LPG under the 2016 policy. The levy was intended to help state-owned entities, including Pakistan State Oil, Parco and Sui Southern Gas Company, import LPG during winter and emergencies. Haider alleged that despite billions of rupees being collected through the levy, these entities had failed to import supplies during the current shortage.
Article Summary: Natural gas available for barely six hours a day in Rawalpindi. Families are increasingly relying on cheaper alternatives such as discarded furniture wood and sawdust. Residents are also facing steep increases in the cost of LPG cylinders, with a new domestic cylinder selling for PKR13,500 (approx Rs 4644)

Article Title: India should arm Afghan Taliban against Pakistan: Sushant Sareen
Article Text:
-

India should consider formally recognising the Taliban government in Afghanistan and providing it with military assistance to counter Pakistan, strategic affairs analyst Sushant Sareen has argued, calling for a rethink of New Delhi’s approach to its western neighbourhood.Speaking on Faultline with Ananya Dasgupta on Times Axis, Sareen said India should not allow international consensus to dictate its Afghanistan policy. He argued that if Pakistan was using military force to pressure the Taliban, India should consider helping the Afghan regime defend itself.“If the Afghan Taliban are going to be bullied by the Pakistanis… then maybe we should help them militarily,” Sareen said. “So that they can also hit back.”He went beyond making a general case for military assistance, suggesting that India consider supplying Afghanistan with anti-drone systems, drone technology and missile capabilities.“If you can give them some anti-drone systems to the Afghans, if you can give them maybe some drone technology, which will help them fight back, maybe give them some missile systems or, you know, long-range rocket systems,” Sareen said.“Why not? I think we should consider it so that at least the Pakistanis cannot, you know, bully somebody into submission,” he added, arguing that India needed to be more willing to take risks if it wanted to project power internationally.Sareen’s argument comes against the backdrop of growing tensions between Pakistan and the Taliban, once backed by Islamabad but now increasingly unwilling to follow its instructions. The conflict has exposed the limits of Pakistan’s long-standing effort to exercise strategic influence over Afghanistan.Sareen said India should also reconsider its refusal to formally recognise the Taliban government, which came to power in 2021. He argued that recognition need not mean approval of the regime’s ideology or policies.“Recognition does not mean endorsement,” he said, pointing out that countries maintain diplomatic relations with governments whose actions they do not necessarily agree with.According to Sareen, the Taliban are the de facto rulers of Afghanistan and India already has a degree of engagement with them. He questioned why New Delhi should continue to hold back from formal recognition simply because other countries have not changed their position.Sareen said New Delhi should make its own assessment of what serves Indian interests, rather than remain constrained by concerns about how other countries might react.“The world doesn't ask us for our opinions before they start doing things,” he said.Sareen believes Pakistan’s Afghan strategy has backfired. Islamabad once viewed the Taliban as a means of securing influence in Afghanistan, but the relationship has turned adversarial as the Taliban has asserted its own interests.Explaining the mistake in Pakistan’s calculations, Sareen said Islamabad had mistaken a temporary alliance with sections of the Afghan population for lasting control.“You can rent an Afghan, you can't buy him,” he said, adding that the Afghans acted in Pakistan’s interests only as long as it suited them. Once they gained greater agency, they began pursuing their own priorities.Pakistan accuses the Taliban of providing sanctuary to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), whose attacks have targeted the Pakistani state. The Taliban, in turn, has resisted pressure from Islamabad and accused Pakistan of backing groups opposed to its rule.Sareen also discussed Pakistan’s interest in the Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghan territory that could provide direct connectivity to Central Asia. He said Pakistan appeared to see control of the corridor as a way to gain strategic leverage over the Taliban, but warned that such a move could invite retaliation.For India, Sareen argued, the question is whether the deteriorating relationship between Pakistan and the Taliban creates an opportunity to protect its own strategic interests. He urged New Delhi to consider both diplomatic recognition and military assistance, while acknowledging that a more assertive role would carry risks.His proposal raises a difficult question for Indian policymakers: could a former Pakistani ally now become a strategic counterweight to Islamabad — and is New Delhi prepared to act on that possibility?
Article Summary: India should not allow international consensus to dictate its Afghanistan policy, says Sushant Sareen. He argues that if Pakistan was using military force to pressure the Taliban, India should consider helping the Afghan regime defend itself. He suggests that India consider supplying Afghanistan with anti-drone systems, drone technology and missile capabilities.

Article Title: ‘Koi sharam hoti hai': Pak lawmaker mocks Khawaja Asif after Munir’s Iran visit
Article Text:
Fazl then turned Asif’s own words against him, repeating a phrase the defence minister had previously used to taunt PTI

Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman took a jibe at Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif over Field Marshal Asim Munir’s participation in a high-level regional security meeting in Iran, questioning why the defence minister was absent from the talks.According to a report by Dawn, Fazl raised the issue during his address to the National Assembly on Wednesday, referring to a meeting in Tehran attended by Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, alongside senior officials from Iran, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.“A defence pact is taking shape in Iran, a meeting is under way (there), and the defence minister is sitting here,” Fazl said, drawing laughter and desk-thumping in the House. Pointing to Naqvi’s presence at the meeting, he asked: “The interior minister is required there as well?”Fazl then turned Asif’s own words against him, repeating a phrase the defence minister had previously used to taunt Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).“There is your respect and stature — koi sharam hoti hai, koi haya hoti hai (have some shame, show some modesty),” he said, breaking into laughter.Responding in the National Assembly on Thursday, Asif denied that a defence pact was being negotiated in Tehran. He said the discussions had nothing to do with Pakistan’s defence or any related matter and argued that Munir had assumed a role focused on maintaining peace and dialogue following last year’s military conflict with India.The meeting brought together Munir, Naqvi, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, alongside senior Iranian officials, to discuss regional security and cooperation.A joint statement issued after the talks said the participants had agreed to continue their dialogue to strengthen cooperation among the four regional countries, particularly on peace and security.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also called for greater regional unity, saying closer cooperation among Muslim nations would help address shared challenges and resist external pressure.
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman took a jibe at Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif over Field Marshal Asim Munir’s participation in a high-level regional security meeting in Iran.

Article Title: Pakistan gas bowser explodes after truck collision, killing 2 and damaging 6 vehicles
Article Text:
Photo for representative purpose only (File)

At least two people were killed and five others critically injured after a gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's southern Sindh province on Wednesday, police said.The accident occurred on the National Highway near Rohri Interchange in Sukkur district. Preliminary reports suggest the gas bowser, which was carrying fuel under pressure, collided at high speed with a heavy trailer.The impact damaged the bowser's tank, triggering a powerful explosion and a fire that spread to nearby vehicles, Xinhua News Agency reported.Police said the two people killed were the driver and cleaner of the gas bowser. Both died at the scene after being caught in the explosion.Rescue teams and emergency services rushed to the site after receiving reports of the blast. The five injured people, who suffered serious burns and other injuries, were taken to a nearby hospital in Sukkur for treatment. Several remained in critical condition, medical personnel said.The explosion and subsequent fire also damaged or destroyed six other vehicles, including two fuel tankers, three heavy cargo trailers and a commercial Mazda truck.Police temporarily halted traffic on the National Highway and cordoned off the area around Rohri Interchange to allow firefighters and rescue teams to operate safely.Authorities began clearing the burnt wreckage and launched an investigation to establish the exact circumstances of the collision.
Article Summary: Gas bowser collided with another heavy vehicle and exploded in Pakistan's southern Sindh province. Police said the two people killed were the driver and cleaner of the gas bowser. Five injured people, who suffered serious burns and other injuries, were taken to a nearby hospital in Sukkur.

Article Title: Pakistan's gas mess: LPG prices soar, imported LNG piles up and the debt bill keeps growing
Article Text:
Expensive cylinders, dwindling reserves: Inside Pakistan's deepening gas crisis

A supply shock ahead of winter

Pakistan faces shortages after Iran war disruption

First, understand the three fuels

Natural gas: Extracted from underground fields and delivered to homes, businesses and factories through pipelines. Pakistan's domestic production has been declining.

LNG: Natural gas cooled into liquid form for transport by ship. After arriving at a terminal, it is converted back into gas, known as regasified LNG or RLNG, and supplied through the network.

LPG: Liquefied petroleum gas, made up mainly of propane and butane. It is stored in cylinders and is especially important for households that do not have piped-gas connections.

Domestic gas is running out faster than new supplies are arriving

Pakistan's domestic gas production falls 20% in five years

The LNG paradox: Too little gas, then too much

A financial hole worth trillions

Pakistan's gas circular debt surges due to supply shortages

Why Pakistan's govt cannot simply raise prices

The crisis reaches far beyond the kitchen

Power sector, households, fertiliser and industry: Who consumes Pakistan's gas?

A domestic LPG cylinder that cost around PKR 4,500 in Pakistan's Balochistan province has shot up to nearly PKR 7,000. In some parts of the country, LPG prices have reached PKR 600 per kg, more than double the official rate. With supplies disrupted following the closure of key border crossings with Iran, households are struggling to find affordable cooking fuel. Some have even begun turning to wood and coal.But the shortage has exposed a much bigger problem. Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining, its dependence on expensive imports has grown, and debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. Yet, even as households struggle with shortages, the country has also been dealing with surplus imported LNG that it cannot easily use or sell.On October 21, 2026, Dawn reported that LPG prices had climbed to as much as PKR 600 per kg in hilly areas and PKR 500 per kg in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, even though the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) had fixed the official October rate at around PKR 279 per kg. The regulator's notified price for an 11.8kg domestic cylinder was PKR 3,296.23.The disruption has since intensified. Reuters reported on October 23 that the closure of the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings with Iran had halted LPG imports, leaving tankers stranded and worsening shortages.Traders said Pakistan imported about 7,000 metric tonnes of LPG a day from Iran. In Balochistan, the price of a 12kg cylinder had risen from around PKR 4,500 to PKR 7,000. Pakistan cited security and anti-smuggling concerns for the border closure, while Iran pointed to technical issues. The two sides were consulting on resuming trade.The pressure is also visible in Rawalpindi and Islamabad. Dawn reported on October 26 that households facing limited piped-gas supply and soaring LPG prices had begun turning to wood and coal for cooking. Residents reported receiving natural gas for only about six hours a day, while LPG was selling at around PKR 600 per kg.Part of the confusion around Pakistan's gas crisis comes from the fact that three different fuels are often discussed as though they are interchangeable.The distinction matters because a disruption in one supply chain does not automatically mean the same thing for the others.The fuels nevertheless compete for the same household energy budget. When piped gas is unavailable or supplied only for a few hours, families turn to LPG. When LPG becomes unaffordable, some shift to wood or coal. The result is that a supply shock in one part of the system can quickly affect everyday life.The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), a government-backed research institution, said domestic gas production fell from 3,597 million cubic feet per day in financial year 2020 to 2,890 million cubic feet per day in FY2025. That is a decline of nearly 20% in five years. PIDE attributed the fall to the depletion of mature fields and a failure of new discoveries to replace the lost output.The Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25 offers another snapshot of the pressure on the system. It recorded average gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet per day during July-March FY2025, including 798 million cubic feet per day of imported RLNG. Domestic gas remained crucial, but imported supplies were already filling a substantial part of the gap.This is not simply a matter of turning up production. Gas exploration requires investment, time and confidence that companies will be paid for what they produce. PIDE has argued that payment delays, distorted price signals and the financial troubles of state-owned gas utilities have weakened incentives for investment. It has also highlighted the damage caused when domestic production is curtailed to make room for imported LNG.Pakistan began importing LNG in 2015 as domestic production became insufficient. Its supply arrangements include long-term contracts with Qatar, one lasting 15 years and another 10 years, as well as an agreement with Italy's Eni. These contracts helped secure supplies, but they also reduced the government's flexibility when demand changed.The problem became particularly visible in 2025. According to the US-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), LNG consumption fell by 1.21 million tonnes that year. Rapid growth in rooftop solar power and weaker demand from the electricity grid contributed to a change in the country's energy requirements.Yet contracted LNG supplies could not be adjusted easily enough to reflect the fall in demand.That left Pakistan facing an unusual predicament: A country struggling with gas shortages could also have more imported LNG than it needed at particular times.With limited storage capacity, surplus LNG had to be diverted into the domestic network or otherwise managed. But imported gas costs more than much of Pakistan's domestically produced gas, while household tariffs have often been kept below the full cost of supply.Diverting expensive imported fuel to consumers at lower regulated rates can therefore create losses rather than solve the underlying financial problem.IEEFA estimated that Pakistan's gas-sector circular debt stood at around PKR 3.3 trillion in its March 2026 assessment. The think tank also said unaccounted-for gas losses, including theft and technical leakages, were estimated at around 11.7% of gas handled.On October 20, Business Recorder reported that federal energy minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had told the National Assembly that Pakistan's total gas-sector circular debt and outstanding payments to domestic gas and LNG suppliers stood at PKR 5.454 trillion as of June 30, 2026.Of this, circular debt accounted for PKR 3.631 trillion, while outstanding payments to gas suppliers amounted to another PKR 1.823 trillion. The minister said the circular debt included PKR 1.448 trillion in tariff differentials, PKR 131 billion in receivables from power companies, PKR 210 billion in sales and income tax receivables, and PKR 59 billion related to litigation.Circular debt builds up when money owed at one point in the supply chain is not paid on time, preventing the next entity from meeting its own obligations. In Pakistan's gas sector, the problem has been aggravated by tariff gaps, unpaid bills, delayed payments and the cost of imported fuel.The consequences extend beyond balance sheets. When gas utilities struggle to recover the cost of supply, their ability to pay producers and maintain infrastructure comes under pressure. Producers, in turn, have less incentive to invest in new fields. Consumers may face higher tariffs, restricted supply or both.The IMF's concerns have continued into 2026. Dawn reported on October 2 that the lender had urged Pakistan to speed up work on targeted gas subsidies and address the sector's rising circular debt. The report said discussions were under way on shifting support from subsidised tariffs towards direct assistance for eligible low-income households, although data and ownership-related problems made the transition difficult.Pakistan's government has tried to balance financial reform with relief for consumers. On January 6, 2026, the Press Information Department reported that petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had announced, on PM Shehbaz Sharif's directions, that gas prices would remain unchanged for six months.The minister also said the government had negotiated with Qatar to divert surplus LNG cargoes to international markets while respecting contractual obligations.But holding tariffs steady does not automatically eliminate the gap between what gas costs and what consumers pay. Nor does it address the separate problem of LPG prices in the open market, where supply disruptions can push prices well above the regulator's notified rate.The Shehbaz Sharif-led government has also considered replacing broad gas subsidies with a single fair price, while protecting vulnerable households through targeted assistance. On August 27, the detroleum division said petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had urged reforms, including steps to curb gas theft, reduce losses and improve revenue recovery at Sui Southern Gas Company.Pakistan's Economic Survey for 2024-25 recorded average daily gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet during July-March FY2025. The power sector accounted for 973 million cubic feet per day, while domestic consumers used 777 million and the fertiliser sector 764 million. General industry consumed another 536 million cubic feet per day.These figures show why gas allocation is such a difficult policy choice. A supply shortfall can affect household cooking and heating, but it can also disrupt electricity generation, fertiliser production and industrial operations.Fertiliser plants are particularly important because their output feeds directly into agriculture. If gas supply or prices disrupt production, the effects can spread through fertiliser availability, farming costs and food prices. Industries that depend on gas for heat, processing or captive power can also face higher costs, potentially weakening competitiveness and investment.Until those structural problems are addressed, temporary relief may ease one winter's hardship without preventing the next shortage. Pakistan's gas crisis is bigger than LPG prices because the cylinder is only where a much wider failure becomes visible.
Article Summary: Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining. The country's dependence on expensive imports has grown. Pakistan's debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. A supply shock in one part of the system can quickly affect everyday life. Gas exploration requires time and confidence that companies will be paid.

Article Title: Afghan returnees face police raids, arbitrary detention in Pakistan's KP after emergency: Report
Article Text:
Emergency in Imran Khan's bastion, fresh fears for Afghan returnees in Pakistan

Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan have reported a rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following the military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in the province, as news agency ANI cited TOLO News report.Returnees said daily life had become increasingly difficult, with Pakistani police frequently searching their homes and restricting their freedom of movement. Several deportees alleged that they were being detained on flimsy pretexts and that law enforcement personnel were demanding bribes in exchange for their release.Mohammad Rahman, an Afghan returnee, told TOLO News that his family had moved from Punjab to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan's tenure in search of better living conditions.However, he said the situation had deteriorated sharply after Islamabad declared an emergency and imposed governor's rule, leaving refugees afraid to step outside for fear of arbitrary arrest and extortion.Another deportee, Sohail Khan, said authorities were conducting raids on residential properties at night while targeting and intimidating refugees in local markets during the day to extract money. Displaced families also recounted being picked up from their workplaces and subjected to humiliating treatment before being deported.The reported crackdown comes as nearly 27,000 Afghan refugees have returned to Afghanistan through the Torkham border terminal over the past three months. Officials at the Omari Temporary Settlement near Torkham said administrative arrangements, including 12 dedicated support committees, remain in place to provide essential assistance and manage a possible increase in arrivals.Meanwhile, efforts to resettle returning Afghans are continuing. The Taliban-led ministry of urban development and housing said more than 74,000 residential plots had been distributed to returning families across 22 provinces.The ministry added that land had been allocated across 27 dedicated townships, with 37 master development plans formally approved to support the reintegration of returnees.The Munir-Sharif duo imposed a state of emergency and governor’s rule in Pakistan’s northwestern province, a stronghold of jailed former PM Imran Khan’s party, PTI.
Article Summary: Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan report rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion. Comes after military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Pakistan reopens Iran border after week-long halt to commercial traffic
Article Text:
Following a week-long closure due to security threats, Pakistan has reopened the Gabd-Rimdan border crossing with Iran.

Security concerns preceded reopening

Pakistan has resumed cross-border trade with Iran through a major border point in Balochistan after a seven-day shutdown disrupted cargo movement, left transporters stranded and raised concerns about LPG availability as winter approaches.Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. according to the news agency PTI.Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, head of the Gwadar chamber of commerce and industry, confirmed that the crossing, also called Gate 250, was operational again.Kalmati said trucks and other vehicles carrying commercial goods were now permitted to travel in both directions between Pakistan and Iran.Welcoming the reopening, he said it would offer relief to traders and transport operators who had been unable to move their cargo during the closure. The restoration of supplies could also help address Pakistan's LPG shortage and ease pressure on rising food and energy costs.The crossing was shut on October 17 by Pakistan's commerce ministry, which did not publicly disclose the reason for the suspension. However, security concerns were believed to have prompted the move.The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases during the colder months.The situation worsened on Thursday when unidentified gunmen attacked trucks parked near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing. Dozens of vehicles were reportedly set ablaze, while several others sustained damage.Local authorities reviewed the security situation before allowing trade to resume on Saturday. Additional security personnel have been deployed to safeguard commercial convoys travelling through the area.The reopening also follows a visit to Iran earlier this week by Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who held discussions with Iranian leaders on bilateral ties and regional developments.Pakistan and Iran share a 909-km frontier between Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan province and Pakistan's Balochistan province. The border crossings are vital channels for trade and the movement of goods between the neighbouring countries.
Article Summary: Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases.

Article Title: 'Islamabad arming Afghans to fight anti-Pakistani insurgents': Ex-US envoy sounds alarm
Article Text:
The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul

Former US envoy Zalmay Khalilzad has sounded the alarm over reports that Islamabad is recruiting Afghans to fight anti-Pakistan insurgents, warning that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further.“There have been many reports that Pakistan is arming Afghans to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. Now there are reports that the Pakistani military is recruiting Afghans to fight against anti-Pakistan insurgents. As things currently stand, relations between #Afghanistan and #Pakistan are likely to get much worse,” Khalilzad wrote.Pakistan's information ministry on Saturday rejected Khalilzad's allegations as “baseless and misleading”, accusing him of promoting a narrative in support of the Taliban government in Afghanistan.The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul, with repeated border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan adding to tensions this year.On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border. Pakistani security officials and state-run media said troops, backed by artillery, destroyed Taliban posts during hours of fighting in Kurram district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Pakistani officials also claimed that troops killed an unspecified number of Pakistani Taliban militants attempting to cross into Pakistan from eastern Afghanistan. Kabul did not immediately comment on the clashes.Pakistan has accused Afghanistan of providing sanctuary to leaders and fighters of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban. Kabul has denied the allegations. The continuing violence has further strained relations between the two countries.
Article Summary: Zalmay Khalilzad warns that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further. The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul. On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border.

Article Title: 'Pak defeated, cannot fight us': Baloch rebels launch fresh strike; several killed
Article Text:
The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces, alleging that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG) during its ongoing Operation Almas.In a press release issued by its spokesperson, Major Gwahram Baloch, the separatist group claimed that Pakistani forces had suffered significant human and material losses at multiple locations and were forced to retreat following clashes. The BLF, as cited by news agency ANI said that the operation was continuing on several fronts with “full intensity and success”.Videos purportedly showing the ongoing violence have also surfaced. In one clip, a woman is heard saying, “Pakistan is defeated now & and cannot fight us”, as gunfire continues in the background. Another video showed a woman firing what appeared to be an assault rifle.The BLF further claimed that its fighters had overrun the main camp of the Frontier Works Organization (FWO) and hoisted the organisation’s flag at Gwadar Zero Point, describing the development as evidence of its advances during the operation.The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station, seizing official weapons and military equipment. It alleged that a police official was killed during the confrontation.In a separate incident in Gubd, the BLF said its fighters attacked a convoy of Pakistani security forces, destroying an army vehicle and killing or injuring several personnel travelling in it. The group also claimed that its fighters had taken control of the police checkpoint at Gubd Cross.
Article Summary: The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces. The group alleges that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG)

Article Title: Pakistan's elite want out? Khawaja Asif flags bureaucrats' alleged exit plans to foreign shores
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan defence minister Khwaja Asif

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats, alleging that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country, according to a report by Pakistan's Express Tribune.In a post on X, Asif said Pakistan had capable and honest bureaucrats, but alleged that many officials had made Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other European countries their permanent homes over the past several years.He claimed some officers had prepared for their relocation under a deliberate plan while employed by the Pakistani government. Portugal, he said, had emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He added that he had raised the issue on social media a few months ago.Asif said the officers whose names had surfaced in connection with the matter had held important positions and remained close to successive governments. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled after collecting substantial sums of money from several influential bureaucrats.The minister did not identify the officials or provide details to substantiate the allegations. He said troubling accounts were circulating about the matter and questioned whether senior officials who had enjoyed the privileges and respect associated with public service had remained committed to Pakistan.“Does it rise above all doubt and suspicion, or are they merely in transit?” Asif asked, questioning whether such officials viewed Pakistan as their permanent home or merely a temporary stop before settling abroad.
Article Summary: Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats. He alleges that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country. Portugal has emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer killed in IED blast during Balochistan operation
Article Text:
Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists.

A Pakistan Army major was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during a security operation in Balochistan province, while security forces killed four terrorists in a separate operation, the military said on Monday.According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, security forces conducted operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Gwadar and Jattakabad in Kalat district on Sunday following reports of terrorist presence.During an operation in Jattakabad, the forces killed four terrorists and recovered “a large cache of arms and ammunition”, the Army said.In a separate action, security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district. During the operation, 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation.“Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area,” the Army said.The military added that security forces and law enforcement agencies remained committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing the four terrorists and expressed grief over the death of the officer.“Major Wajahat Waheed sacrificed his life for the protection of our beloved homeland; the nation is proud of its brave son,” the prime minister said.Sharif also extended condolences to the officer's family and prayed for the elevation of his rank.Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, with security forces continuing operations to contain the violence.A day earlier, security forces killed eight terrorists during operations in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts.(With inputs from PTI)
Article Summary: Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists. Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation. Security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district.

Article Title: US-designated LeT terrorist dies after mysteriously falling from building in Lahore
Article Text:
LeT terrorist Chaudhary Muhammed Sarwar.

NEW DELHI: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim, one of the founding members of the outfit, died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday.The incident reminded of a similar death that had occurred in 2016 when fake currency kingpin, Javed Khanani, had died after falling from an under construction building in Karachi.Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League. He was a close aide of both Hafiz Saeed and current deputy chief Saifullah Kasuri. Sarwar's son had also died in a road accident a few months ago.It was in 2016 tha Sarwar was designated a terrorist by the US justice department who termed himself as a senior LeT memeber in Lahore active since early 2000s, holding various leadership roles in the group. At the time, he was LeT’s emir for Lahore, a position he has held since at least January 2015."As the LeT emir of Lahore, Sarwar maintains relationships with LeT’s most senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, Sarwar worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, and in early 2013, Makki asked Sarwar for money to pay for his travel within Pakistan," the US justice department had said in its statement."Sarwar had been directly involved in LeT fundraising activities and used the formal financial system in Pakistan to raise and move funds on behalf of LeT. For example, in 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities for the purpose of soliciting donations for the group," it added.
Article Summary: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday. Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League.

Article Title: Pakistani forces kill 8 militants in Balochistan, raid hideouts as abductions rise
Article Text:
The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas (Photo: ANI).

Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid rising cases of abduction in the troubled region.The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas, according to the Inter Service Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistan Army.In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists trying to set up a roadblock to disrupt local traffic were "intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five terrorists", the ISPR said in a statement.In Nushki district, security forces stormed a hideout, and two terrorists were killed in an intense exchange of fire, the army said. Around 500 kilograms of explosives were also recovered from the terrorists during that operation. In Khuzdar district, one terrorist was killed, the ISPR added.Balochistan, which borders Afghanistan, has seen a surge in abductions and attacks on civilians and securityforces in recent years, prompting the government to step up its anti-militant operations.On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers near Mastung, on the Quetta-Karachi highway, and took them away. Their whereabouts remain unknown.On Sunday, at least 18 workers were abducted, and another was injured when unidentified armed men attacked a marble mining site in the province. The incident happened early in the morning in the remote Naal area of Khuzdar district, police said. The attackers arrived on motorcycles and other vehicles and stormed the site.According to PTI, no insurgent group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack.The police and the provincial government have yet to confirm the incident officially, but two police officers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said 18 workers had been taken away by the attackers. PTI reported."They came on bikes and vehicles and opened fire and then rounded up the workers present at the site and abducted 18 of them before fleeing," a police officer said.Most of those abducted came from nearby villages and areas, he added, and another worker was injured in the attack.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces reportedly kill eight militants in three intelligence- led operations across districts of Balochistan province. Operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas. On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers.

Article Title: Pakistan’s decades of backing terror comes full circle as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls under emergency rule
Article Text:
The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.

Decades of militant policy and blowback

Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authority

Opposition crackdown deepens rights concerns

Tribal communities face renewed uncertainty

Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control.
