It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Pakistani Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains. A report by news agency ANI highlights how this policy has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.Pakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward.As stated in the report, the state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark, “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.The imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.The intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. While the state faces a persistent militant threat, its response has further narrowed the space for political opposition and public dissent.The latest intervention has also placed additional pressure on communities that have endured years of displacement and insecurity. Past military operations, including Zarb-e-Azb and Radd-ul-Fasad, remain associated with civilian hardship and human rights concerns.Thousands of displaced families are still awaiting return and rehabilitation. For these communities, the emergency raises fears of another period of disruption, particularly as the authorities expand their control and military involvement in civilian affairs.The consequences of Pakistan’s security policies have thus extended beyond the fight against armed groups. Tribal populations have faced displacement, civilian casualties and prolonged instability, while the failure to resolve the underlying conflict has left many vulnerable to further intervention.The emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brings these tensions into sharper focus. A state that has long relied on militant groups to pursue strategic objectives now faces the consequences of violence within its own borders. Its response, however, has centred on expanding federal control, weakening elected authority and restricting opposition activity.Rather than resolving the crisis, the latest measures risk deepening the divide between the state and the communities it claims to protect. The removal of an elected provincial government, the concentration of power in unelected institutions and the crackdown on dissent point to a broader struggle over Pakistan’s democratic future, even as the country confronts the long-term fallout of its militant policies.
Article Summary: Emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) It comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers.

Article Title: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response on whereabouts of Barman from Bangladesh
Article Text:
Barman came on medical visa for treatment at Siliguri in West Bengal on March 20 last year, attended the hospital for two days, then went to Thakur Anukul Chandra Ashram at Deoghar and is untraceable since March 24 last year.

NEW DELHI: Bipul Chandra Barman, a resident of ‘Hindu Prodhan Para’ in Panchagarh district of Bangladesh, came on medical visa for treatment at Siliguri in West Bengal on March 20 last year, attended the hospital for two days, then went to Thakur Anukul Chandra Ashram at Deoghar and is untraceable since March 24 last year.For the ministry of external affairs (MEA), additional solicitor general Archana Pathak Dave informed the Supreme Court, which has in session of a habeas corpus petition by Barman’s wife in session, that the person remains untraceable and that the relatives must lodge a zero FIR relating to a missing person complaint with Jharkhand police at Deoghar.The wife, through her counsel, said on Jun 30 last year, the Bangladesh High Commission in Kolkata, acting on a request from MEA, issued a letter to the Bangladesh government seeking verification of a person detained in India and identified as Bipul Chandra Pradhan. In August last year, the Bangladesh foreign ministry sent a letter to the Indian home ministry confirming that Barman is a Bangladeshi citizen and has no criminal antecedents.In search of her husband, the wife travelled to India and gave representation for Barman’s release in June this year. Finding no response, she moved the SC.What was intriguing for the SC was the categorical denial by the MEA that Barman has neither been detained, arrested, nor deported by Indian authorities and that his status remains as a missing person.Dave also informed the court that Indian authorities have not communicated at all with the Bangladesh counterparts on Barman.Adding further complications to an already complicated case, the West Bengal government informed the court that Barman’s mobile phone number was found to be used by a person at Barh in Bihar, which is proximate to Deoghar in Jharkhand, the place he visited last before becoming untraceable.The CDR analysis showed his last known location was at a temple in Matigara, a place near Siliguri.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the ASG, who informed the Bangladesh Deputy High Commissioner about the detention of Barman and sought verification of his citizenship and antecedents. SC directed the Union government to file a detailed status report after examining all the leads given in the petition and the status report filed by the West Bengal government.
Article Summary: Bipul Chandra Barman, a resident of ‘Hindu Prodhan Para’ in Panchagarh district of Bangladesh, came on medical visa for treatment at Siliguri in West Bengal on March 20 last year. He attended the hospital for two days, then went to Thakur Anukul Chandra Ashram at Deoghar and is untraceable since March 24.

Article Title: Nepal foots Rs 10 lakh rescue bill for 6 Indians trekking illegally despite warnings
Article Text:
A drone view shows houses covered in mud after the flash floods and mudslide, at Devighat. (Reuters file photo)

TOI

Nepal spent an estimated Rs 10 lakh (INR) from its disaster management fund to rescue six Indian trekkers who had allegedly entered the restricted Upper Dolpa region without mandatory permits, ignored warnings against travelling during heavy snowfall and pressed ahead, leaving their guide behind.The group, comprising five trekkers from West Bengal and one from Andhra Pradesh, spent two nights stranded in the mountains before a helicopter evacuated them on Monday. Authorities subsequently charged them NPR 1.6 lakh (approximately Rs 98,000) in permit fees and penalties but reduced the fines considering their physical condition after the ordeal.The six trekkers — Moumita Halder, Piyali Koley, Jajla Trivedi Kumar, Aditya Singha, Diplina Biswas and Rajesh De — were rescued at dawn on Monday from Danigad, around 300km northwest of Kathmandu. The helicopter made three round trips, evacuating two trekkers on each round. All six were taken to Dunai, the Dolpa district headquarters, where they underwent medical examinations and were subsequently discharged. The operation required a civilian helicopter after a Nepal Army aircraft scheduled to arrive on Sunday developed a technical problem and could not fly.Dolpa chief district officer Junu Hamal toldthat authorities could have imposed a maximum fine of NPR 50,000 (Rs 31,250) on each trekker but instead charged NPR 20,000 (Rs 12,500) per person.The trekkers also paid $40 (Rs 3,800) each towards mandatory permits. "Seeing their condition, we gave them a concession," Hamal said. However, she criticised the group for ignoring repeated warnings from security personnel, local residents and their guide, putting both themselves and rescuers at risk."Such irresponsible behaviour is unacceptable," she said. "Nepal is already struggling to find funds for reconstruction after the devastating flash floods on Aug 26. At a time when we are trying to rebuild affected communities, having to spend precious disaster funds on a rescue necessitated by such carelessness and irresponsible behaviour is extremely frustrating," she said.The district administration had restricted travel to Upper Dolpa from Oct 29 because of heavy snowfall, but the trekkers allegedly left their guide behind and continued towards Shey-Phoksundo lake despite warnings. They became stranded near the Numa La and Baga La mountain passes, and their guide alerted authorities on Saturday evening. Snow and poor mobile connectivity complicated rescue efforts. The remote terrain and snowbound passes made a ground rescue difficult, leaving helicopter evacuation as the practical option.
Article Summary: The group, comprising five trekkers from West Bengal and one from Andhra Pradesh, spent two nights stranded in the mountains. Authorities subsequently charged them NPR 1.6 lakh (approximately Rs 98,000) in permit fees and penalties but reduced the fines considering their physical condition after the ordeal.

Article Title: 'Act responsibly': Taliban urges US over planned deportation of Afghan immigrants
Article Text:
Afghan deportees to be sent via Pakistan? Taliban urges US to act responsibly

The Afghan Taliban government on Monday urged the United States to "act responsibly" while deporting Afghan immigrants back home, saying Kabul was prepared to engage constructively with Washington on the issue, news agency Reuters reported.The statement came amid plans by US President Donald Trump 's administration to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan, according to a US official and a coalition of veterans and advocacy groups cited by Reuters on Friday."The Afghan side is prepared, while understanding the existing realities and taking into consideration the legitimate interests of both sides, to engage constructively and on the basis of mutual understanding in this regard," the Afghan Taliban foreign ministry said in a statement.More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, the New York Times reported on Friday, adding that the first flight could take place as early as Monday.The deportations are expected to be routed through Pakistan , as Washington cannot directly arrange deportations to Afghanistan due to its lack of diplomatic ties with the Taliban government."Third countries should not treat the citizens of another country as a matter of bargaining in exchange for limited temporary concessions or other considerations", the Afghan statement said.Pakistan and Afghanistan have been at odds over militant attacks, with Islamabad accusing Kabul of harbouring militants who stage cross-border attacks. Kabul has denied the charge.
Article Summary: Afghan Taliban government urges U.S. to "act responsibly" while deporting Afghan immigrants back home. Statement came amid plans by US President Donald Trump's administration to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan. More than 150 Afghan immigrants are expected to be deported, the New York Times reported.

Article Title: Violent protests rock Bangladesh garment hubs as workers demand a steep pay hike
Article Text:
Police used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse crowds as demonstrations intensified. (Reuters)

What's the demand

Wage board formed, but protests continue

Violent protests have erupted in Bangladesh's garment industry as workers demand a sharp increase in their minimum monthly wage from 12,500 taka to 30,000 taka. Clashes, vandalism and road blockades have been reported in Dhaka and Gazipur, prompting authorities to deploy police and Border Guard Bangladesh personnel to restore order.The unrest, which began on Saturday, escalated on Sunday in industrial areas such as Mirpur in Dhaka and Konabari in Gazipur. Protesters allegedly vandalised factories, attacked police outposts with stones and set police vehicles on fire. Several major roads were blocked using barricades, disrupting movement.Police used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse crowds as demonstrations intensified. Border Guard Bangladesh units were also deployed alongside police to maintain security in the affected areas.Garment workers are demanding a monthly minimum wage of 30,000 taka, more than twice the existing minimum of 12,500 taka. Their demand comes amid a recent government announcement of a new pay scale for public sector employees, which is expected to nearly double their salaries and benefits.Workers are seeking a comparable improvement in their earnings, arguing for a substantial increase in wages. However, factory owners say they are struggling with declining orders, stagnant product prices and rising costs of imported raw materials.They have argued that meeting the workers' demand would be difficult under current conditions.The Bangladesh government has formed a wage board to decide on a revised minimum wage for garment workers. However, the move has not brought the demonstrations to an end, with workers continuing to protest for higher pay.The dispute has put the spotlight on Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) industry, which grew rapidly from the late 1970s and early 1980s to become the backbone of the country's export economy.The sector accounts for more than 80 per cent of Bangladesh's export earnings and employs around four million people. Women make up an estimated 60 to 70 per cent of its workforce, making the industry a major source of employment and economic opportunity for them.
Article Summary: Clashes, vandalism and road blockades have been reported in Dhaka and Gazipur. Protesters allegedly vandalised factories, attacked police outposts with stones and set police vehicles on fire. Police used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse crowds as demonstrations intensified.

Article Title: Six Indian tourists go missing during trek to Nepal's Shey-Phoksundo Lake
Article Text:
Heavy snowfall in Nepal: Six Indian tourists go missing during trek

Search and rescue ops under way

Over 240 tourists in Upper Dolpa

Six Indian tourists, including two women and four men, have gone missing during a trek to Nepal's Shey-Phoksundo Lake, the deepest lake in the country, following heavy snowfall in the Himalayan region, officials confirmed to news agency ANI.The tourists were travelling from Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Dolpo Buddha Rural Municipality towards the lake when they went missing. They were last reported to be in the Numla Pass and Bagla Pass areas between Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality.Local guides suspect that the tourists may have become stranded in the mountains following heavy snowfall, reportedly influenced by Cyclone Arnab developing over the Bay of Bengal.According to local officials, the group continued its journey despite warnings from residents about difficult weather and dangerous conditions along the mountain passes. They are believed to have become trapped in the snow while returning from the high-altitude area.Dolpa chief district officer Junu Hamal confirmed that the tourists were stranded while returning from Dho towards Phoksundo Lake."The tourists became stranded while returning from Dho towards Phoksundo Lake," Hamal said, adding that locals had warned them about the difficult weather and mountain conditions before they proceeded.Shey-Phoksundo Rural Municipality Chairman Dhawa Samduk Gurung said the lack of mobile phone connectivity in the mountain passes had made it difficult to establish contact with the missing tourists."Mobile phone communication is unavailable in the mountain passes between Wards 4 and 8, making it difficult to obtain information about the tourists' whereabouts and current condition," Gurung said.Authorities have initiated efforts to trace the missing tourists, but heavy snowfall and adverse weather conditions have hampered search and rescue operations in the high-altitude region.Dolpa deputy superintendent of police Anil Raj Giri said the six Indian tourists remained uncontactable as per the latest information."Six Indian tourists remain out of contact, according to the latest information," Giri said.He added that authorities had requested the concerned agency to arrange a helicopter to assist in search and rescue operations.A team of the Nepal army has also been deployed to locate the tourists and help with the rescue efforts.The absence of mobile connectivity, thick snow and difficult terrain have made it challenging for rescue teams to establish the group's exact location and assess their condition.According to the District Administration Office, 244 tourists have reached Upper Dolpa. They include 149 Nepali nationals, 44 tourists from SAARC countries and 51 visitors from other foreign countries.Amid the worsening weather conditions, the district administration has urged tourists to avoid risky areas and remain in safe locations.Tourist arrivals in the Shey-Phoksundo Lake region have increased in recent years. Official data show that 4,882 tourists visited Phoksundo Lake during the first 11 months of the fiscal year 2082/83.
Article Summary: Six Indian tourists, including two women and four men, have gone missing during a trek to Nepal's Shey-Phoksundo Lake. The tourists were travelling from Ward Nos. 4 and 8 of Dolpo Buddha Rural Municipality towards the lake when they went missing. They are believed to have become trapped in the snow while returning from the high-altitude area.
